name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri Democrats gain ground in polls, but congressional races remain uphill battles
text:
The U.S. Capitol building in Washington, D.C., amid fog on Dec. 10, 2024 (Jennifer Shutt/States Newsroom).Missouri Republicans’ advantage among voters has narrowed sharply this year, but that shift may do little to change the state’s congressional delegation on Nov. 3. 
An August St. Louis University/YouGov survey showed Missourians were just about evenly split between Republicans and Democrats on a generic congressional ballot, a major gain for Democrats from a poll in February. 
But Democratic voters are mainly concentrated in the 1st and 5th districts. Republicans won the other six by comfortable margins in 2024 and there’s only one race that has attracted significant broadcast advertising: The 2nd District in eastern Missouri.
Incumbent U.S. Rep. Ann Wagner raised $562,000 from mid-July through Sept. 30 and spent $2.4 million in that period defending her seat. She has spent $1.2 million on broadcast ads so far, according to tracking by The Independent. Her Democratic opponent, Fred Wellman, outraised Wagner in the period by more than $200,000 but was outspent by an almost 6-to-1 margin.
Wellman  has spent only $271,000 on broadcast advertising.
Wagner, a longtime figure in Missouri Republican politics, is seeking her eighth term. Wellman, a retired military officer, is making his first bid for office.
U.S Rep. Ann Wagner at a news conference on Aug. 2, 2018 in Washington, DC. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images).
Interviews with voters in the district revealed sharply different views of national politics. Kay Wiese of Ballwin told The Independent she believes suburban swing voters are souring on Republicans. 
“There’s not a lot of thoughtful input from a lot of the folks that we have on the Republican side,” she said. “I feel like they are mostly puppets in that party. It’s just like they are not standing up for the middle class, the more common people.”
But Pat Compton of Winchester said she sees no reason to change her support for Republicans. While many voters are angry over high gas prices, she is not.
“I’m for the war in Iran,” Compton said. “Once that gets settled, the prices will change.”
The 2nd District is the most competitive congressional race in Missouri, according to Cook Political Report. It is rated as “Likely Republican” while the other seven districts are rated as “solid” for the incumbent party.
On the west side of Missouri, intense battles for seats in Congress are playing out on television — but the ads are for races in Kansas. 
Republicans did try to make another Missouri congressional district competitive this year, but not through campaign advertising.
Last year, Republican lawmakers redrew six of Missouri’s eight congressional districts in an effort to flip the Democratic-held 5th District in Kansas City. But a referendum campaign put the 2025 map on the Nov. 3 ballot, and the courts blocked its use in this year’s election.
It took a ruling from the Missouri Supreme Court on Sept. 3, affirmed three times by the U.S. Supreme Court, to end the GOP’s effort to use the 2025 map in November alongside the referendum.
The Republican nominee in the district — state Sen. Rick Brattin — struggled to raise money in September, when the redistricting plan was in dispute in state and federal courts. 
A campaign disclosure report filed this week shows Brattin raised only $900 in the five days after the U.S. Supreme Court’s Sept. 25 decision. His last significant promotional expense was $2,855 for yard signs on the day of the Missouri Supreme Court ruling.
Uncertain congressional map hangs over Missouri’s crowded 5th District GOP primary

The court decisions severely diminished the value of the Republican nomination.
If the 2025 boundaries had been used in November, the district would have been rated as solidly Republican. President Donald Trump won the votes in those boundaries by 18%, according to Cook Political Report. The incumbent, Democratic U.S. Rep. Emanuel Cleaver, won his 2024 re-election in the boundaries that will be used in November with 60% of the vote.
In the aftermath, Brattin lashed out.
“The responsibility for this chaos rests first and foremost with the Missouri Supreme Court,” Brattin wrote on social media.
Cleaver, as expected, praised the courts.
“For more than a year, state officials have spent precious time, energy, and resources on an effort to silence the voices of Missouri voters and steal a congressional seat,” Cleaver said on social media. 
Instead of a potentially competitive, multimillion-dollar campaign, Brattin now finds himself in the same position as most challengers to Missouri incumbents this year: short on money and facing long odds.
He reported having $17,503 on hand on Sept. 30.
Josh Smead, Democratic candidate for Congress in Missouri’s 6th District, greets voters Oct. 10 along the route of the Brunswick Pecan Festival parade (Rudi Keller/Missouri Independent).
There is little in the way of campaign activity in any other district that would suggest Missouri will not return incumbents — or the incumbent party nominee — to Washington. Incumbents and nominees of the incumbent party have raised 89% of the money for this year’s contests and had 94% of the funds available on Oct. 1.
The ballot lineups in Missouri’s six remaining congressional races are:

1st District, St. Louis and St. Louis County: U.S. Rep. Wesley Bell won renomination for a second term in a primary rematch with former U.S. Rep. Cori Bush, whom he unseated in 2024. Paul Berry III is on the Republican ticket and has not formed a campaign committee.
3rd District, Central Missouri to St. Charles and Jefferson counties: U.S. Rep. Bob Onder of Lake Saint Louis, a Republican seeking his second term against Democratic nominee Bethany Mann. Onder had $568,000 on hand and Mann had about $10,000 on hand in the most recent reports.
4th District, Central Missouri to the Kansas border, including Whiteman Air Force Base and Fort Leonard Wood. U.S. Rep. Mark Alford is a Republican seeking his third term, with Democratic nominee Jordan Herrera and Libertarian Thomas Holbrook on the ballot. Alford had $773,000 on hand and Holbrook had $3,125 at the most recent report.
6th District, north Missouri from St. Joseph to Hannibal. Chris Stigall won the Republican nomination to replace U.S. Rep. Sam Graves. His Democratic opponent, Josh Smead, is doing better than some rural district Democrats in fundraising — he made a small broadcast ad buy — but Stigall had $212,000 on hand at the last report compared to $32,156 for Smead.
7th District, southwest Missouri including Springfield, Joplin and Branson. U.S. Rep. Eric Burlison is seeking his third term in office in the district that has been Republican the longest in Missouri. His Democratic opponent, Missi Hesketh, had $33,543 on hand at the latest report while Burlison reported $961,193. Libertarian Kevin Craig has not reported raising any money.
8th District, southeast Missouri from Rolla and Jefferson County to the Bootheel. U.S. Rep. Jason Smith, chairman of the House Ways and Means Committee, is seeking his sixth full term. The Republican won a special election in 2013. He had almost  $5.5 million on hand on Sept. 30, while Democratic challenger Chris Reichard had $12,563. Libertarian Rebecca Sharpe Lombard has not formed a campaign committee.

Democrats are hoping to link Republicans to unpopular state policies and the SLU/YouGov poll offered a potential sign of weakness for the GOP in northwest Missouri. Voters in the region favored Democrats 46% to 35% on a generic congressional ballot, though the regional sample of just 52 respondents makes it difficult to draw firm conclusions.
The region, which includes St. Joseph, showed an 11-point preference for Democrats on a generic ballot.
Just to the south, Platte County is a battleground for Missouri House seats. Voter Eric Munch said he backs the redistricting plan and Republicans.
Platte County is in the 6th District and the 2025 map did not change that.
“I don’t have any problem with it,” Munch told The Independent. “The state voted in a Republican Legislature, and if they want to go after redistricting, I say go for it.”
The last Democrat representing a largely rural congressional district, the late U.S. Rep. Ike Skelton of Lexington, lost his office in 2010 after 17 terms. For Democrats to translate their statewide gains into congressional victories, they will have to win back some of the rural voters who abandoned the party over the past two decades.
The lack of money doesn’t keep most underdog candidates from working crowds and visiting the events that matter in communities in their district. Smead walked in the Brunswick Pecan Festival Parade in Chariton County on Oct. 3 while Stigall stayed away.
As he waited for the parade, James Ostermann, a Chariton County farmer, blamed high diesel prices on a lack of refining capacity and faulted Democrats’ environmental policies for limiting development.
“I used to be Democrat straight through, but they put so much pressure on the middle class and everybody that they’ve just taken my vote away,” Ostermann said.
That attitude may be softening, said Grace Fortner of Keytesville. 
She said she returned to her home county about 10 years ago to raise her family.
“I don’t think that’s true, simply because I’m looking around my county and my district lately, and it’s the first year I feel hope for our district actually,” Fortner said. “This is the best I’ve ever seen Democrats’ signs out and around in the last 10 years, especially the last eight years.”

name: Missouri Independent
title: Six years in, The Missouri Independent is growing because of you
text:
Missouri State Capitol building in Jefferson City (Getty Images).Six years ago, when we launched The Missouri Independent, I made what was probably a pretty lousy sales pitch.
Don’t trust us. Not yet, anyway.
I asked Missourians to judge us by our work. To hold us accountable for our promises. To make us prove that we really were, as legendary investigative reporter Wayne Barrett once put it, “detectives for the people.”
It was easy enough to make those promises in October 2020. We were a brand-new nonprofit newsroom with four journalists and some pretty big ambitions.
Living up to them was going to be the hard part.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As The Independent celebrates its sixth anniversary this week, I look at what our team has built and find it hard to believe how far we’ve come. But the thing I’m most proud of isn’t how much we’ve grown. It’s that we’ve been able to grow without abandoning the promise we made on day one.
Relentless investigative journalism. Daily reporting that helps Missourians understand their government and the people who run it. And all of it free. No paywall. No advertising.
That’s been our mission from the beginning.
Consider what happened just a few weeks ago.
Two of our reporters, Clara Bates and Anna Spoerre, won the Missouri Press Association’s A-Mark Prize for Investigative Journalism for their reporting on Missouri’s troubled foster care system.
Their work exposed how children languish in state custody, how inadequate legal representation can leave families trapped in the system and how a young woman who spent nearly her entire life in foster care had to fight the state to keep her own baby.
I’m proud of the award. I’m even prouder of the journalism that earned it.
Because those stories took time. They required tracking down records, earning the trust of vulnerable people, asking uncomfortable questions and refusing to accept easy answers.
That’s what investigative reporting is supposed to look like. And it’s exactly the kind of work we promised to do six years ago.
It’s also the kind of work that costs money.
And because of the people who believe in our mission, we’re able to do more of it.
Earlier this month, we announced a partnership with ProPublica, one of the country’s premier investigative news organizations, that brought veteran reporter Luke Nozicka into our newsroom.
Luke has a track record of accountability reporting, including investigations that helped free an innocent man from prison and exposed racial discrimination within the Kansas City Police Department.
With Luke’s arrival, our team has expanded from four journalists in 2020 to seven today.
We’ve also expanded beyond the written word.
Last month, in partnership with Missourinet, we launched Missouri on the Record, a weekly podcast designed to take listeners beyond the headlines.
The goal is simple: Give Missourians more context about the stories shaping their state, introduce them to the people behind those stories and hopefully reach audiences who might never have stumbled across our website.
And we continue to see our journalism published and broadcast by newspapers, television stations and radio outlets across Missouri.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
We don’t believe important journalism should be confined to the people who know where to look for it. A story about state government belongs just as much to someone reading their hometown newspaper in the Bootheel as it does to someone checking our website in St. Louis or Kansas City.
So we give our work away. Other news organizations can republish it for free, extending the reach of our reporting well beyond our own audience.
And none of it happens without you.
We depend on readers who believe that journalism is a public good worth investing in. Even small contributions matter enormously.
Five dollars a month may not sound like much. But when enough people make that commitment, it adds up. It helps pay for reporting trips, public records requests and the time it takes to pursue a story when the people in power would rather we move along.
And if donating isn’t in the cards, there’s another way you can make a real difference.
Share our free morning newsletter with friends and family. Forward it. Encourage someone to sign up. At a time when social media algorithms increasingly determine which stories people see, our newsletter gives us a direct line to readers. And every new subscriber means one more Missourian who doesn’t have to depend on a tech company to decide whether our journalism is worth seeing.
I know there are plenty of people who don’t trust journalists. Some never will. And I’m not asking for blind faith now any more than I did six years ago.
Read our work. Challenge us when we get something wrong. Tell us what we’re missing. Hold us to the standards we’ve set for ourselves.
More than a century ago, Walter Williams, the founding dean of the Missouri School of Journalism, wrote in his Journalist’s Creed that “the supreme test of good journalism is the measure of its public service.”
That’s the standard we’ve tried to live up to.
And six years ago, I asked you to hold us to our promises.
I hope you never stop.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Myth busting, values voting, Maine messaging
text:
Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen leads a news conference announcing he will seek changes to how Nebraska oversees the federal Temporary Assistance for Needy Families program for low-income families on Friday, Oct. 9, 2026, in the Nebraska State Capitol. (Photo courtesy of Gov. Jim Pillen's office)Three thoughts … 
Whether Nebraska wants to be like Florida is an open question. I’m a hard pass, but when the feds OK’d a plan to put the kibosh on certain kinds of spending for Nebraskans receiving Temporary Assistance for Needy Families’ Aid to Dependent Children funds, we became the second state they approved. Florida was the first.
The over 2,800 Nebraska households that get the $4,700 monthly TANF benefit — numbers courtesy of DHHS — will now be unable to spend any of it on items such as porn, pot or the ponies. Of course, nobody offered any evidence that they already did. 
Those getting the monthly TANF stipend now have a longer list of no-nos including smoking products, intoxicants, entertainment, tattoos or piercings, spa treatments, psychics, anything to do with gambling including lottery tickets, video games, pornography, jewelry or, my favorite, political contributions.
The rationale makes some sense. SNAP beneficiaries already have limits on what they can purchase, although a recent court ruling in Nebraska allowed them to continue to buy candy, soft drinks and energy drinks with SNAP funds. 
The underlying argument the government has been making the last couple of years is that we are awash in “waste, fraud and abuse” of public funds. Indeed, the misadventure we know as DOGE (Department of Government Efficiency) promised taxpayer savings of $2 trillion but delivered only about $175 billion, a number some believe is even overinflated. On the way, DOGE did away with USAID, reducing the nation’s standing in the world, and fired 284,000 federal employees.
Still “waste, fraud and abuse” remains a rallying cry for the administration and its supporters, some of whom have offices in the Capitol but live in Nebraska ZIP codes. While no one wants tax dollars wasted, obtained fraudulently or abused by recipients, according to economists from the American Enterprise Institute to the feds’ own Government Accounting Office, most of the money lost is not through individual fraud but rather through clerical or administrative errors. For example, according to the U.S. Department of Agriculture, the fraud rate for SNAP is less than 1.5% and its overall payment rate error is less than 7%. 
Keeping such numbers in perspective belies this myth: That low-income Americans, 70% of whom work full-time jobs — some for companies worth billions — yet still need help feeding their families, are somehow the problem in the “waste, fraud and abuse” calculus.
***
We don’t hear much about values voters anymore, although my guess is they still are out there, voting their values. A Values Voter Summit used to be held each fall, the last of which was hosted by the Family Research Council in 2020. I never understood the concept. Don’t we all vote our values? Even if a candidate gets my vote because I like his hair or she wears my favorite color, my vote indicates what I value, however shallow.
I thought about values voting as I tried to wrap my mind around another school shooting, this one in Bend, Oregon, during the same week that a plan to livestream the firing-squad execution of a mass murderer was nixed.
Four people were murdered in the Bend shooting, three students and a teacher. Two others were wounded. The 16-year-old identified as the shooter was killed by a bystander.
Much has been written about what has become our apparent indifference toward gun violence and school shootings. The evidence of such insouciance? No real progress has been made toward any solutions, and gun violence remains the leading cause of death for children in America.
And while I’m pleased that the secretary of defense’s plan to turn an execution into a public spectacle was canceled, the thinking behind it remains part of our cultural bloodstream.
All of which makes a voter wonder just what it is we do value?
***
Nebraskans and Mainers share at least one political characteristic in that we both decide our Electoral College votes by congressional district rather than winner-take-all. Perhaps we’ve found another.
A recent debate in the Pine Tree State between GOP incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and her opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, was held before a live audience at Husson University in Bangor. Near the end of the occasionally testy debate, an audience member started shouting at Collins about data centers ruining their state.
Collins quickly tried to portray the heckler as a Jackson supporter, a charge to which Jackson replied, “Oh, just shut up!”
For those of us in the Cornhusker State (and surely the other 49) weary of a parade of incessant and mostly insipid political ads airing on television, arriving in our inboxes, appearing on our caller IDs and showing up in our text messages, we couldn’t have said it better ourselves.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Who funded Nebraska Working People, America First parties? Law doesn’t require disclosure.
text:
John Cartier of Lincoln, left, and Robin Richards of Ralston respectively led creation of the America First Party and Nebraska Working People Party and served as the inaugural chairs of the parties. Richards is also the 2026 U.S. Senate nominee for her party. (Photos courtesy of John Cartier, Robin Richards and the respective political parties | Nebraska Capitol photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Candidates and ballot-measure campaigns petitioning to appear on Nebraska’s ballot must disclose how much is spent on signature gathering. 
But Nebraska law doesn’t require new political parties to disclose their finances until they are qualified to have candidates on the ballot. 
For 2026, that leaves a gap of at least two months of reporting for the new Nebraska Working People Party and America First Party that likely will never be disclosed for signature gathering or litigation, unless party officials voluntarily disclose the information. 
The Working People Party said it won’t, and one party official cited the lack of transparency in his resignation. By an Oct. 5 reporting deadline, neither party had filed a state disclosure report.
“This cycle has shown us that absolutely this is an area where money is going to be spent to impact politics in meaningful ways that Nebraskans want to know about, but they can’t right now. They can’t do anything,” Gavin Geis, executive director of Common Cause Nebraska, told the Nebraska Examiner.
‘Law doesn’t really contemplate this’
Geis said he’s fielded questions “again and again” about who funded the creation of the two new state political parties this summer.
Gavin Geis, executive director of Common Cause Nebraska. (Photo courtesy of Common Cause Nebraska)
“I have to tell them time and again, ‘I’m sorry, but the law doesn’t really contemplate this,’” Geis said.
Laws regulating campaign finance are different for the Nebraska Accountability and Disclosure Commission, for the state, and the Federal Election Commission, for federal candidates.
In Nebraska, the reporting threshold is $5,000 raised or spent toward the goal of being elected and/or supporting or opposing ballot questions.


NADC 2026 election campaign finance
State disclosures mean detailed info on finances between Jan. 1, 2025, and Sept. 29, 2026, for some of Nebraska’s most expensive state-level races, including some breaking state records:

Nebraska governor: $14.73 million raised, $10.22 million spent.
Initiative Measures 440 and 441, to legalize and regulate online sports betting: $14.65 million raised, $9.22 million spent.
Nebraska’s 25 legislative races (total): $7.81 million raised, $4.95 million spent.
Initiative Measure 442, to cement part of a state law dealing with sex and K-12 and collegiate sports in the Nebraska Constitution: $3.1 million raised, $3.02 million spent.
Nebraska attorney general: $1.93 million raised, $1.08 million spent.
Nebraska’s three University of Nebraska Board of Regents races (total): $1.8 million raised, $1.03 million spent.



An Examiner review of petitions for the two new political parties showed most of the thousands of signatures, if not all, came from paid circulators. 
Some circulators were from Nebraska, but a few dozen hailed from out of state, including Arizona, California, Florida, Georgia, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, Mississippi, Missouri, Montana, Nevada, New York, North Carolina, Ohio, Oklahoma, Oregon, Tennessee and Texas.
Geis said he can understand why this issue wasn’t pondered sooner. The tactic of forming new political parties as a strategy could be new, he said, and it remains to be seen whether the tactic is successful this November or whether it will be repeated in Nebraska or elsewhere.
“You can’t really wave it aside and say, ‘Oh, it doesn’t have any impact.’ It clearly does,” Geis said. “People are clearly watching and curious and want to know more.”
Parties certified Aug. 26
The NADC, the state agency overseeing campaign finance for Nebraska candidates and issues, confirmed in a July 21 email that under state law, a political party is only considered a “committee” for campaign finance disclosure purposes once it qualifies for the ballot.
County election officials validated nearly 18,000 signatures across the two campaigns. The two measures both needed about 2,200 signatures apiece across each of Nebraska’s three congressional districts to qualify for the ballot.
The Nebraska Republican Party and Nebraska Democratic Party each sued to block the new parties after signature gathering. The NEGOP and NDP argued the newcomers could sow confusion. The Nebraska Supreme Court ultimately upheld the new parties in an Aug. 26 ruling. 
Outgoing Secretary of State Bob Evnen certified the parties that afternoon, which became the starting point for money raised (including leftover money) or spent toward the $5,000 limit.
The first reporting deadline for the 2026 general election was Oct. 5, covering June 16-Sept. 29 for candidates and political parties.
But by then, neither of the new parties reported raising or spending more than $5,000.
By Sept. 1, eight candidates petitioned to appear on the ballot for the new parties, three for the Nebraska Working People and five for America First. State law only required valid signatures from at least 25 new party members to appear on the ballot for each office.
Should the law be changed?
Of more than a dozen state senators the Examiner spoke to over the past three months about the disclosure requirements, all said they were unaware the parties would not be required to disclose finances from the signature-gathering or initial litigation period.
State Sens. Christy Armendariz of Omaha, left, Paul Strommen of Sidney, center and Mike Jacobson of North Platte meet on the floor of the Nebraska Legislature. Jan. 29, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Paul Strommen of Sidney, one of many lawmakers who have scrutinized petition campaign finance, said he was concerned about various types of “dark money” in Nebraska. He said the issue for political parties, among others, should be looked at in 2027.
Evnen, a member of the NADC by virtue of his office, said the parties will need to honor the $5,000 threshold. Asked if he would support disclosure changes, Evnen said on Sept. 3: “Haven’t considered it, but I would.”
State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha, who will be term-limited next January, said this is clearly a “blind spot” that should be rectified.
State Sen. Margo Juarez of Omaha said she was surprised and that the law needed to change. State Sen. Tony Sorrentino of Elkhorn said in the 11 seconds or so he considered the matter after being informed by the Examiner, it seemed inequitable. He wondered whether the matter had ever been brought up in the Legislature.
Marijuana supporters twice petitioned to create a new party, first in 2016 — the Nebraska Marijuana Party — and again in 2020 after the first effort fell short. In early 2021, the Legal Marijuana NOW Party joined Republicans, Democrats and Libertarians as a valid state party.
State Sen. Margo Juarez of Omaha. April 8, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
However, unlike before, the Nebraska Working People and America First parties appeared this summer without a prior push. This year also features the tense race for U.S. Senate featuring Democrats pledging to back registered nonpartisan Dan Osborn for U.S. Senate against U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, a Republican, and going as far to clear their ballot line to help Osborn. 
Ricketts and Osborn also face candidates for the Legal Marijuana NOW (whose candidate dropped out in August), Nebraska Working People and America First parties.
‘Vitriol, harassment and political retaliation’
The NADC confirmed nothing prevents the America First or Nebraska Working People parties from voluntarily disclosing their finances. 
However, in August, Robin Richards, the chair of the Nebraska Working People Party, who would later become the party’s U.S. Senate nominee, said that wouldn’t happen.
U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., center, faces Robin Richards of Ralston, left, of the Nebraska Working People Party, nonpartisan Dan Osborn, right, and Dan Hartong of the America First Party, not pictured, in Nebraska’s Senate race in 2026. Also not pictured: Mike Marvin of Omaha, nominee for the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, and Chuck Conboy of Papillion, candidate for the America First Party. Marvin suspended his race in August but will still appear on the ballot. (Candidate photos courtesy of respective campaigns | U.S. Capitol photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)
Richards, who ran a write-in campaign for Legislative District 12 in the spring, described her party as being “made possible by a broad base of supporters who believe Nebraskans deserve a meaningful alternative to the two established parties.”
“Because of the level of vitriol, harassment and political retaliation surrounding this effort, all of those supporters have asked to remain anonymous, and we intend to honor their request,” she said in an Aug. 21 email.
“We will comply fully with every disclosure requirement under Nebraska law,” Richards continued. “At the same time, we will not voluntarily expose private citizens to harassment simply because they chose to support the creation of a new political party. The focus should remain on the thousands of Nebraskans who signed our petitions and the reasons they believe our current political system is no longer working for them.”
The Nebraska Democratic Party, in a July 19 email to party members, ran the subject line: “Betrayal by fellow DEM w/ MAGA backing could cost us the Senate.” The email described Richards as “disgruntled” after she lost her legislative race and endorsed incumbent Republican state Sen. Merv Riepe over the runner-up Democrat, Christy Knorr. Richards came runner-up for the same seat in 2022, losing to Riepe by 524 votes. The party added: “There is no doubt this is the work of shadowy MAGA operatives, using a turncoat Democrat as the poster child.”
Party officers resign
The Nebraska Working People Party’s initial treasurer, Vince Rukstalis, resigned just three days after the party qualified for the ballot. The vice chair, Joe Hunter, also resigned. Hunter, a former Democrat, is running for Papillion mayor. Rukstalis is a registered Republican.
Petition pages reviewed by local county election officials and returned to the Nebraska Secretary of State’s Office sit in the office for public inspection at the office’s Elections Division in downtown Lincoln on Aug. 24, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Rukstalis, in a resignation email to Richards, which he posted online, said he fully supports the party’s basic premise. However, he said he never imagined the party would run a federal-level candidate, or that Richards herself would be a nominee. He said the “distraction” from Hunter and his campaign was too much and that he was “taking all the hits while no one else is.”
“Furthermore, I cannot in good conscience continue in any executive capacity while still having zero information or understanding about full visibility and transparency into the funding source after repeatedly having asked about this critical piece of information,” Rukstalis wrote.
“In conclusion, you now have a certified party to run, and most likely a Senate race. Your benefactors, whoever they are, will expect you to fully engage to meet their expectations. Clearly, this was all well-planned in advance, executed very precisely and seemingly at Joe’s expense.”
‘Basic paperwork’
NEGOP Chair Mary Jane Truemper criticized the America First Party in an Oct. 7 statement for supposedly not raising $5,000 by Sept. 29 and for its gubernatorial nominee, former state Sen. Brett Lindstrom of Omaha, missing a reporting deadline by three days. 
“If they can’t handle basic paperwork or raise a dime, they have no business asking Nebraskans to hand them the keys to our state,” Truemper said in the statement. “Voters will see this sham of a party for what it is and choose common sense in November.”
Nebraska Republican Party Chair Mary Jane Truemper, center in green, at a 2026 midterms rally in Grand Island, Nebraska, on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, at the Nebraska State Fairgrounds with thousands in attendance featuring President Donald Trump. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
John Cartier, the chair of the America First Party, declined multiple requests for comments to the Examiner but fired back at Truemper within hours of the party’s post.
He questioned how much money the GOP had spent to keep his party off the ballot and argued that if the America First Party was “so irrelevant, why did they fight so hard to keep Nebraskans from having the option to vote for us?”
Cartier, a former Democrat who also helped the Legal Marijuana NOW Party, including being treasurer for that party’s 2026 Senate nominee, has tried to attract wayward Republicans to his party. He also blasted Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen, U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts and other Republicans for what Cartier said were governance actions that defied “common sense,” as Truemper put it.
“If you’re asking for receipts, there’s a pretty big mess sitting right in front of you,” Cartier wrote. “See you in November!”
‘A very poor choice’
Cavanaugh and Juarez, both Democrats, said they were dismayed that neither new party would voluntarily disclose its information, even if not required.
“They’re newly established parties — already they want to start off not being transparent? Why? Why is that a good first step?” Juarez said. “I think it’s a very poor choice.”
State Sens. John Fredrickson of Omaha, Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha and Merv Riepe of Ralston. Jan. 7, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Cavanaugh has publicly questioned the rumor mill, including Nebraska Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb and others directly who asserted, without evidence, that Ricketts was behind Richards’ new party. “For whatever reason,” Cavanaugh said, her asking questions seemed to have “ignited theories” that she was considering joining either party or being one of their candidates. Both of those points, she said, aren’t true.
“I was saying I’d like to see the evidence that Pete Ricketts is behind it, because it just seemed like a fabrication based on no evidence,” Cavanaugh said. 
‘Nobody has concrete evidence’
Geis said disclosure has the added benefit of preventing some of the “wild speculation” around the new parties, instead firmly answering whether an effort is more grassroots or revealing whether major donors or operatives are at play.
“Either way, I think transparency would allow voters to stop assuming the worst and know the truth of who is looking to influence our elections,” Geis said.
Nebraska  Democratic Party Chair Jane Kleeb at the Omaha Hilton on Nov. 8, 2025. At left is former President Joe Biden. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
Kleeb, speaking with the Examiner on Aug. 21, repeatedly pointed fingers at allies close to Ricketts or Richards as behind the signature gathering. 
Asked what evidence she had regarding Ricketts’ involvement, Kleeb responded: “Nobody has concrete evidence, because there’s no campaign disclosures.”
Kleeb went on to say that it’s a “very small political world.”
“It’s a very disgusting, shady business, and it’s shameful that they don’t have to disclose this information,” Kleeb said.
‘Stop blaming everyone else’
Jessica Flanagain, a partner at Axiom Strategies and key Ricketts ally whom Kleeb accused of being involved, denied involvement and said Kleeb was at the center of “all the new-party, no-party nonsense.”
Axiom Strategy’s Jessica Flanagain carries signs for Nebraska U.S. Sen. Pete Ricketts, R-Neb., after an event at the Washington County Fairgrounds. Oct. 19, 2025. (Photo by Juan Salinas II/Nebraska Examiner)
“First, she manipulated the Democrat primary to help Dan Osborn. Then one of her own failed Democrat candidates launched the Working People’s Party. Then a professional activist the Democrats once endorsed answered with a desperate America First Party,” Flanagain said in an Aug. 21 text.
“This will haunt the Democrat Party for years,” she continued. “Jane needs to stop blaming everyone else and get her own house in order.”
Truemper similarly denied the Republican Party’s involvement in the petition effort. The campaigns for Osborn and Ricketts have also repeatedly denied involvement.
Getting the ‘full picture’
Geis said that, in talking with his counterparts in other states, he learned this “gap” is not unique to Nebraska. At the same time, he said, political party formation as a strategy hasn’t been as “aggressive” elsewhere.
“We may be experiencing something novel, which explains the lack of regulation,” Geis said in a follow-up email.
The 2026 election has already been a confusing cycle, Geis added, and he said voters should have as much information as they can to help them make informed decisions, including requiring more of actors who, at times, hope to sow more confusion.
“I don’t know if that is both of these parties’ goal, but I think the end result is the same, that Nebraskans don’t really understand what’s going on or how they get the information to get a better picture,” Geis said. “It should fall to the state, at the end of the day, to make sure that they (Nebraskans) can get that full picture.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Foreign policy drives demands for accountability from House candidates in NJ
text:
Democratic and GOP candidates in next month's midterm elections have called for more scrutiny of direct foreign aid and money spent to fight wars. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]Foreign policy has taken an outsized role in the run-up to next month’s midterm elections, as candidates and voters alike increasingly blame the Iran war and new tariffs for worsening affordability at home and debate whether Israel is using U.S. aid to fight terrorism or wipe out Gaza.
In New Jersey, even Republicans who have been longtime loyalists to President Donald Trump fear the impact his foreign policy will have at the polls Nov. 3, as his approval ratings sink to new lows.
“He’s going to kill all of us in midterms,” said Republican Damon Galdo, who’s challenging Rep. Donald Norcross (D) in South Jersey’s 1st District. “Trump made a promise that gas prices would be low, he’d ‘drill baby drill,’ and then we get into this conflict, and gas prices are through the roof.”
In some ways, candidates running to represent New Jersey in Congress next year have not strayed far from their parties’ broad positions on Israel, Iran, and beyond.
Republicans cite concerns about Iran developing nuclear weapons to justify Trump’s actions there and regard aid to Israel and its military actions in the region as necessary to defend democracy in the Middle East.
Democrats blast Trump’s tendency to barge into international conflicts without Congress’ consent or consideration of the long-term implications, while the party’s more left-leaning factions have protested Israel’s attacks in Gaza as genocidal and demanded Israeli leaders be held accountable.
Yet Democratic and Republican candidates have called for more scrutiny of both direct foreign aid and money spent to fight wars as voters grow more anxious about the economy.
“It feels as though this government is much more focused on taking from the people here at home, while it’s at the same time giving to people overseas, and that doesn’t align with the needs of my constituents,” said Rachel Peace, a Democrat hoping to flip the 4th District Rep. Chris Smith (R) has held since 1981.
Galdo seconded that sentiment, saying: “We can’t be like an endless ATM.”
They also warn that Trump’s actions abroad have alienated allies, deepened discord globally, and radicalized a new generation of extremists.
“When you bomb a school and 120 kids die, all of those kids have fathers and older brothers. That is going to be a problem in the future. Those people don’t forget,” said Zack Mullock, a Democrat hoping to unseat Rep. Jeff Van Drew (R) in South Jersey’s 2nd District.
Most candidates want the war in Iran to end soon without sending in U.S. troops, but few see a sure path to that goal.
“We can continue to move towards victory the way we have been through our technology superiority and our drone and air superiority,” said Republican Joe Hathaway, a Republican hoping to unseat Rep. Analilia Mejia (D) in North Jersey’s 11th District. “I don’t believe we should be putting U.S. service members on the ground in Iran.”
Mejia and Adam Hamawy, a Democrat running to replace the retiring Rep. Bonnie Watson Coleman in Central Jersey’s 12th District, support impeaching Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who has been roundly criticized for his handling of the Iran war.
U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, a Republican who represents Kentucky, filed a resolution last month accusing Hegseth of violating Congress’ war powers, carrying out extrajudicial killings, and failing to minimize civilian casualties, among other things. But House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican from Louisiana, sent members on recess until after the midterms, preventing a vote.
“I think there are some concerns within the caucus, the broader Democratic caucus, that, you know, we can’t get dragged into impeachment proceedings and instead we should focus on affordability. But I think that it is, we can walk and chew gum,” Mejia said.
Economists estimate the war, which started in February, has cost the average American household $2,000 so far, primarily by driving up energy costs.
On foreign aid, candidates have split opinions.
Israel has been the largest recipient of U.S. aid since World War II, collecting more than $300 billion since 1946, mostly in military aid, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.
Hathaway regards such U.S. support as warranted, calling Israel our lone democratic ally in the Middle East.
“They are a huge economic partner to us as well, I think a $50 billion trade partner across the board. They share our democratic values. Oh, and by the way, they’re surrounded by other nations who would see them eradicated from the face of the Earth, and many of those same nations would see Americans eradicated from the face of the Earth,” Hathaway said. “So it is critically important that we stand in lockstep with our allies in Israel.”
Rep. Josh Gottheimer, a Democrat looking to retain the 5th District seat he has held since 2017, also has been a staunch supporter of Israel.
He has called for unconditional aid, denounced Palestinian solidarity college encampments and high school protests as antisemitic, and introduced legislation to bar U.S. aid to the United Nations until that group declares Hamas and Hezbollah terrorist groups.
During a recent event marking the third anniversary of the Hamas attack on Israel, Gottheimer said: “We will speak the truth about October 7th. We will stand up to hate, wherever it rears its ugly head. And we will never stop fighting for the day when Hamas lays down its arms for good, and communities can live in peace free from terror.”
But other candidates, including Gottheimer’s Republican challenger, Sean Kirrane, believe aid to Israel should get a closer look.
Kirrane applauded the hold a top Democrat on the House Foreign Affairs Committee recently placed on the Trump administration’s $2.8 billion plan to sell Israel 40,000 one-ton bombs.
“That actually makes me happy because it shows me that there are some controls in place, and that someone is actually looking over their shoulder and just not handing out bombs and weapons,” Kirrane said.
As a businessman with a forensic auditing background, Kirrane said he supports audits of all government spending. Federal spending, including on foreign aid, is “not supportable by our GDP, and it’s not supportable by our tax base,” he added.
“If it can’t pass an audit, just like in corporate America, the program should be shut down or stalled until it can, and the people running the program should be held accountable for that,” Kirrane said.
Republican Michael McGuire, who’s challenging Rep. Herb Conaway (D) in Central Jersey’s 3rd District, echoed that sentiment.
“If you’re ever giving anyone money, you have a right to make sure it’s going to the proper channels, 100%,” McGuire said.
Any country that receives U.S. aid should submit to whatever restrictions America sets, with lawmakers taking their cues from the public, Mullock agreed.
“We have a democracy where we vote on what our tax dollars are used for, or at least vote for the folks who decide that,” Mullock said. “So I’m not writing anybody a blank check.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma’s GOP Legislature left out key info on property taxes state question: the financial impact
text:
The downtown Oklahoma City skyline is pictured. (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)If any emoji best represents the property tax state question Oklahoma lawmakers have placed before voters, it would be the grimace.
For those who need a translation, we use that face to express tension. In this case, it’s because our Republican-controlled Legislature, in all its wisdom, tacked on this disclaimer to their proposed constitutional amendment: “If passed, this measure would have a fiscal impact on the state, but the exact impact is unknown.”
(Insert eye-roll emoji.)
Lawmakers, in their zest to convince us they are cutting taxes as inflation rages on, decided that taking the time to suss out how eliminating a chunk of revenue via State Question 847 will affect senior citizens, public schools, CareerTechs, counties and some municipalities wasn’t as important as having a talking point on the campaign trail.
Because that’s where our property taxes go. Reminder: property taxes typically fund the functions of municipal and county governments. State government doesn’t get a dime from these taxes.  
Maybe that’s why they weren’t sure about the fiscal impact?
I don’t know whether this oversight was sheer laziness, a blatant disregard for voter intelligence or if legislators’ effort was a rush job that overlooked the finer details – including how complicated it probably is to calculate the impact.
But in any case, this is an unfair scenario for Oklahoma voters who have to make a decision on Nov. 3 about whether to change the structure of our property tax system. Voters deserve to have all the facts ahead of time, and lawmakers should not be permitted to omit them.
Since they did, though, I’ll fill in the gaps.
An Oklahoma Tax Commission analysis estimates local jurisdictions would lose about $45.78 million in revenue in the first year if voters approve this question. Over the next 10 years, that lost revenue could top $450 million.
That’s a whopping sum of money for a ballot measure that lists its fiscal impact as being “unknown.”
State Question 847 is one of the most convoluted and complicated state questions on the ballot this year, and that’s saying a lot given some of the other issues that lawmakers have placed before voters. (Who can forget that manufacturing tax credit that voters soundly rejected in August?)
Right now, the fair cash value of a home can’t increase by more than 3% a year for homesteads — better known as the homes we own and live in — and for most agricultural land. Commercial property values are capped at no more than a 5% annual increase.
Lawmakers have decided it’s time to lower that cap to a seemingly random 1.75% a year for homesteads and agricultural properties and to 4% for commercial properties. 
They also have decided to muck around with the income cap that senior citizens must meet to qualify for a valuation freeze. The amount of the increase would be calculated on a tiered system ranging from 0% to 1.75% based on a formula that is way too complicated.
Supporters argue that the measure would create the “lowest cap on growth” for homesteads in the U.S. and save cash-strapped Oklahomans money.
Critics, though, point out that besides the previously mentioned budget cuts for public schools, CareerTechs, county governments and some municipalities, it would also make it harder for those entities to borrow money for future needs.
They say this is not really property tax relief. The value of properties will continue to go up, and so will Oklahoman’s taxes. This merely just slows the rate of growth a bit.
But they also warn that because it will reduce revenue, many Oklahomans should expect to see their tax rates go up to pay the existing bills.
That’s because bond debt – that borrowed money I just mentioned – will not miraculously vanish. All bonds are set based on the revenue expected to be generated from existing property taxes. When someone screws around with the formula, it messes up those expected revenue streams.
The only feasible way right now to make up that lost revenue is to adjust the millage rates — better known as the tax rate assessed on real estate. That means everyone will see an increase in their taxes, but I suspect senior citizens living on fixed incomes could feel the pinch more.
Lower-income senior citizens’ home valuations have long been frozen to provide them an idea of what their tax bills will look like each year. Most probably have not budgeted to abruptly pay higher taxes.
How much millage rates will increase depends on how reliant an entity is on the revenue source and whether local jurisdictions have enough resources to adjust. 
Rural residents in particular will likely be harder hit because those entities have less resources to draw on. 
So instead of cutting expenses at the state government level that they control, lawmakers plan to force those cuts on local governments. How is that fair?
Oklahomans’ wallets definitely need relief from soaring property insurance and utility rates as well as high gas, diesel and grocery prices, but this plan doesn’t do anything to address that.
Maybe rather than monkeying around with our property tax formulas, lawmakers should first look at why their policies have resulted in us having the highest homeowners insurance rates in the country — more than double the national average. Reducing those rates would certainly provide welcome relief without harming our local revenue streams.
But it seems like state leaders prefer to live in a fairy tale where instead of apples or peaches, money grows on trees for the benefit of our cities and towns. And instead of doing the hard work of confronting insurance lobbyists and fixing broken state spending, it’s easier to ask voters to pass a plan with an unknown budgetary impact.
Here’s the reality: No business wants to come to a community that doesn’t have good schools, good roads and bridges and solid public services. Those services are primarily paid for by property taxes. 
To put this plan back in emoji speak: big red question mark.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV native teaching next generation about products made in state, bringing supply chain back home
text:
Ed Ryan, founder of Reshore WV, speaks to lawmakers at the West Virginia State Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia on Sept. 14, 2026, about his college course on import substitution and manufacturing. (Photo by Will Price/West Virginia Legislative Photography)A West Virginia native with expertise in trade operations is taking his passion to state college campuses, hoping to connect the upcoming workforce with skills to bring supply chains back home.
There’s a goal, too, of keeping more students in state to curb the population decline, particularly among young adults. 
The initiative has earned the support of many in the Statehouse, including House Speaker Roger Hanshaw. 
There’s nothing but an upside to it, he said.
House Speaker Roger Hanshaw, R-Clay. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
“We need to do everything that we possibly can to help students, young people, aspiring entrepreneurs and potential founders of companies here in West Virginia see what the scope of the possible is,” said Hanshaw, R-Clay. 
Ed Ryan, who grew up in Nitro, is the brainchild behind the economic and education initiative, Reshore WV, and his company, Reshore Technologies.
He has a background in U.S. customs and international logistics and worked outside of the state before returning home.   
Ryan said that initially, he wasn’t “a great student.” Professors at Marshall University introduced him to international relations, Chinese world history and economics.
“I learned to love learning, and fell in love with international trade and economics and world affairs and how trade is this unifying force that can end wars. It has such a power on people,” Ryan said. “I thought, ‘I’m not gonna let any of that go to waste’ and try and do as much as I can here to help companies and communities.”
Products made in West Virginia are on display at the West Virginia Manufacturers Association headquarters in Charleston, West Virginia, on Oct. 16, 2026. (Photo by Amelia Ferrell Knisely/West Virginia Watch)
West Virginia has a wealth of products made in the state, including well-known exports like coal, engines and car parts made at the Buffalo Toyota plant, glass, HVAC filters, aircraft parts, wood products and more. 
Aluminum plates from the Artemis II spacecraft were made by Constellium in Jackson County, and recently earned the honor of “Coolest Thing Made in West Virginia” by the West Virginia Manufacturers Association.
West Virginia companies don’t always know of the resources made in their backyard, opting to import needed products from overseas. Ryan’s work focuses on identifying products West Virginia companies currently purchase overseas and connecting those buyers with manufacturers making those products in state or that have the capability to.
Next, he took that passion to the classroom, first teaching a class at the University of Charleston in spring of last year to MBA students. The course focused on import substitution and manufacturing.
“I think with this curriculum, we’re going to build just so many knowledgeable students who think about maybe not a career in manufacturing, but understanding how manufacturing can then connect to what they do,” Ryan said. “Whether they’re a finance major, a supply chain major, an education major, a marketing major, it just opens up manufacturing … We have thousands of students here in West Virginia that I think this education could benefit.”
Students prepared an import substitution proposal connecting a West Virginia manufacturer product to a real import demand of an in-state company. Students compared costs of importing the product versus purchasing it in-state.
Kelton Boblits
Kelton Boblits, a Fayetteville, West Virginia native and MBA student at U.C., wants a future career in West Virginia after interning at the state Department of Economic Development. Ryan’s course opened Boblit’s eyes to in-state manufacturing possibilities. 
“I had studied supply chains and international commerce in different classes, but this was a seven-week deep dive, and so to get that understanding was valuable,” he said. “Not only that, to find out that the manufacturing base that we have here in West Virginia, I think that that’s something that’s very meaningful … I think if people were to take a look at what is here, they would be very impressed, and I think it would break a lot of stereotypes.”
Ryan has now taken the course to West Virginia University and will soon expand it statewide through a partnership with the West Virginia Higher Education Policy Commission.
Ryan also shared his idea with state lawmakers at the Capitol, explaining how this education is valuable to students statewide.
“Our customer base does not have to be limited to just the 1.8 million West Virginians,” Hanshaw said. “We have to think at least regionally, if not nationally and globally. What Ed and his team are doing in helping to expose young people to those kinds of opportunities is really awesome.”
Del. Lori Dittman, R-Braxton. (Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)
Del. Lori Dittman, R-Braxton, is chair of the House of Delegates’ Higher Education Subcommittee. Dittman, who works at a middle school, praised Ryan for returning to West Virginia and investing in the state. 
“I just think anytime you have students that can get their experience outside of just the text, or just outside of this theoretical learning, and they are actually doing it, that is an incredible experience for them,” she said. “It will help them build a life and a career and be able to stay in West Virginia, and then it’s going to help our West Virginia manufacturers either expand or they’re going to see new ones created because of the demand for the products that are needed.”
Boblits said hundreds of students across West Virginia participating in the course and drafting usable proposals is likely to produce a real impact on the state’s economy.
“They will hit a home run and change their communities for the better, and that’s the impact that I see that’s having on the state long term … It’s going to create opportunity,” he said. 
Reshoring tax credit bill expected in 2027 
Tariff policies from the Trump administration and escalation in supply chain vulnerability played a role in Ryan creating his company in West Virginia, along with his desire to raise his family in the Mountain State. 
Businesses operating in West Virginia imported approximately $4.8 billion in foreign manufactured goods during the calendar year 2024.
Ryan estimated that 15% of West Virginia imports could be substituted for in-state products. 
In the 2027 legislative session, Ryan will be advocating for the “West Virginia Reshore Manufacturing Act,” which creates a tax credit to incentivize the replacement of imported goods with goods manufactured in West Virginia.
“We want to create an economic incentive for a West Virginia company to make that change when it makes sense,” Ryan explained.



Quotation







I think if people were to take a look at what is here, they would be very impressed, and I think it would break a lot of stereotypes.


– Kelton Boblits


The bill was introduced by two Republican senators in the last legislative session, but didn’t make it to the governor’s desk. 
Lawmakers have been working on it since then, according to Hanshaw. Economic development will again be a focus in the House of Delegates next year. 
“If we have the capacity to make it here, and you bring that demand back here, we’ll provide you with a credit of some sort against one or more of the taxes that you pay just for the just for the the benefit of having brought that manufacturing demand back here to West Virginia,” Hanshaw said. 
The speaker said he’s an “enthusiastic supporter” of Ryan’s work with Reshore WV.
“Hats off to Ed and his team for launching it, and I’m really proud of the companies that are taking advantage of it too,” Hanshaw said. “I love everything about this. It’s the kind of thing we got to really be leaning into.”
Kentucky recently launched its own reshoring initiative, drawing on the experiences of Ryan and Reshore WV. Manufacturing leaders in Kentucky credited Ryan for his expertise and work in West Virginia as they launched their initiative on Oct. 14.

name: WyoFile
title: Lawmakers advance draft bill to close legal loopholes for giving alcohol to minors
text:
LANDER—As things currently stand in the state of Wyoming, adults can at times provide alcohol to minors without consequence. A minor may end up in legal trouble for underage drinking — but the adult who supplied the minor with alcohol, if the two are related or the alcohol was consumed for religious or medical purposes, often walks away without a charge. 
Meanwhile, the youth faces a misdemeanor citation.
Fremont County Youth Services representatives have previously reported that some of the kids in the county report drinking at a very young age. It’s not just a countywide problem, Wyoming Highway Patrol Colonel KC Ramsey told the Legislature’s Select Committee on Tribal Relations that there’s a cultural drinking problem in Wyoming.
After hearing about the issue earlier this year, the committee directed the Legislative Service Office to draft legislation to tighten up, if not close, some of those legal loopholes. The bill draft LSO brought back doesn’t remove the exceptions, but it does place a limit on them.

Sen. Cale Case, R-Lander, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

“I think untangling the list of exceptions … that would be very divisive,” said Sen. Cale Case, R-Lander, committee co-chairman. “I do think this is an intelligent and clever way to approach this, and I appreciate it.”
The limit suggested by the bill is a minor’s blood-alcohol content of 0.02%. Below that, the exemptions for parents, legal guardians, religious uses, and medical uses would still apply. Above that, the adult or adults providing alcohol to the minor could face a misdemeanor citation of their own.
“The way the law reads … is a prohibition against any person selling, furnishing or causing to be sold alcohol, and then there are some exceptions to that rule. So in this case, if a minor is above a 0.02%, then it is the person who furnished that alcohol who no longer gets the exception,” LSO’s Ian Shaw explained.
According to Alcohol.org’s blood alcohol calculator, for a 130-pound boy approximately half a glass of wine, or about 2.5 ounces, would likely result in a blood-alcohol content of 0.02%; for a full glass of wine or one 12-ounce beer, the blood alcohol content is estimated to likely fall to 0.02% within about an hour. Most NyQuil is about 10% alcohol by volume, a little less than a standard glass of wine; the standard dose of NyQuil is just over one ounce.
Half a glass of wine is significantly more than is typically used in religious ceremonies. 
Since the bill draft proposes that its new lack of exceptions kick in only if a minor’s blood-alcohol content is over 0.02%, it is unlikely that consumption of a small amount of wine or other alcohol for religious or medical purposes would place a minor over that legal limit.
And, Ramsey assured, the Highway Patrol would not stake out churches or places of worship to try to catch people. As it does now, he said, Highway Patrol would look for signs of intoxication, which would prompt testing as part of a traffic stop. That is to say, the way the bill is currently written it would not alter investigation procedures, only what the consequences of that investigation might be.
“It’s another way for us to ensure that the highways are safe,” he said.
Ramsey originally phrased the Highway Patrol’s position on the bill draft as neutral. After some probing from committee members, including Case and Rep. Pepper Ottman, R-Riverton, he said that the agency regards it as a positive step – but implied that unless it shifts the cultural needle, it may not be the silver bullet that solves underage drinking in Wyoming.
The committee had invited a number of law enforcement agencies to attend and comment on the bill draft, including the Bureau of Indian Affairs, the Fremont County Sheriff’s Office, the Riverton Police Department, and the Lander Police Department as well as the Highway Patrol. Ramsey was the only law enforcement officer who provided comment on the bill.
Sen. Tim Salazar, R-Riverton, expressed some reservations around the bill draft, noting that he feels it’s important to ensure that exceptions are carved out for things like religious use. Nonetheless, he voted in favor of the committee sponsoring the bill.

Sen. Tim Salazar, R-Riverton, during the 2026 Wyoming Legislature budget session in Cheyenne. (Mike Vanata for WyoFile)

Case said the bill strikes the right balance between allowing some exceptions and holding adults responsible when they provide minors with opportunities for excessive consumption. 
“It’s the best of all worlds in this,” he observed. “I mean you’re really not exactly going after the kids, you’re going after the person that did it in an irresponsible manner. If you have a house party … people really get intoxicated, then you’re no longer covered by the exception.”
Case moved for the committee to move the bill forward; Ottman seconded him. Despite his reservations, Salazar voted in favor of advancing the bill, as did committee Co-chairman Rep. Ivan Posey, D-Fort Washakie.
“I’m going to vote yes today, but I’m eager to hear the conversations come January,” Salazar said. “I do need the exceptions in this bill. I need them.”

name: WyoFile
title: A problem with our ‘them’ and ‘us’ mentality
text:
All good people agree, And all good people say, All nice people, like Us, are We And everyone else is They.” — Rudyard Kipling

Opinion

To date, more than 230 people have been killed by our armed forces in the Caribbean. They were presumed to be drug smugglers, but there has been no process whatsoever to assess their guilt. How do we account for this outrage? Even the criminals slaughtered for entertainment in Rome’s Colosseum had been adjudicated. 
Human use of mood-altering substances and psychotropic drugs goes back thousands of years. After the Civil War, unregulated opiates flooded the country to treat the war wounded, and addiction became epidemic. Our government attempted to rein in this problem by passing the Harrison Narcotic Act in 1914. This federal law sharply reduced the legal supply of narcotics. This had the effect of making most attempts to obtain narcotics illegal, and created the problem of “those” people and “those” drugs. 
The furor over “those” people and “those” drugs reached a peak in 2023 when over 70,000 people in the U.S. died from fentanyl overdose. This led to the chapter of the “narcoterrorist” in our War on Drugs. However, this number is dwarfed by 178,000 deaths from beverage alcohol and 480,000 deaths from tobacco in the United States that year. 
In Wyoming that year, 50 people died from fentanyl overdose; 178 people died as a direct consequence of drinking alcohol; and indirect deaths from alcohol totaled 48 from alcohol-related motor vehicle accidents and 57 from suicide. One-third of people who died by suicide test positive for alcohol. The day after heavy drinking there is a seven-fold increase in suicidal behavior. 
A fundamental truth is that legality does not protect from lethality. The separation of mood-altering substances into legal and illegal has created a “them and us” construct. There are many problems with this construct, and the War on Drugs is a big one. So far this war has cost us $1 trillion with 60% going to incarceration, 20% to interdiction and 20% to treatment. 
A commonality between legal and illegal drugs is that human beings have feelings — physical and emotional. Some people use chemicals to alter these feelings. Not infrequently, they have problems with the chemicals they use. 
What you see in life often depends on where you sit. I possessed the unique perspective of a board-certified dermatologist who was also trained and certified in addiction medicine. I saw that there was little difference between people who had been using the wrong substance to treat an itch and made their problems worse, and those who treated their physical or emotional issues with mood-altering substances and made their problems much much worse. 
The solutions for the former were much easier. I became a voluntary combatant in this drug war in 1989, and was involved with community, tribal and professional treatment programs. I witnessed over and over the astounding similarities in the nature of the problems of addiction. Whether the drug is illegal or legal, upper, downer, all-arounder, whether the person is rich or poor, educated or not, white, black, Native American, it’s all the same. What differs most is the availability of support and treatment. The 80% of drug war dollars currently being spent on interdiction and incarceration are largely wasted. 
Interdiction addresses the supply side of this war. We hear that X tons of drugs and XX dollars are seized. Although this gives the impression that our government is doing something, there is always an adequate supply. Even C.J. Box thinks they can make fentanyl in the Bighorn Mountains. 
Incarceration manifests the thinking that the problem is “those” people and “those” drugs. Some 43% of federal inmates and 20% of state inmates are there on drug charges, with minority populations disproportionately represented in prison populations — “those people.” 
Addiction to illegal or legal drugs is a giant health problem. Right now, the greatest health and social problems in the state of Wyoming are legal drugs: alcohol and tobacco. The slaughter in the Caribbean won’t fix these, but just turn our heads elsewhere. Politicians and the media feed on each other, focusing us on “those” people and “those” drugs. 
Humanity has an endemic addiction problem; we need humane solutions. A strong step in the right direction is to protect and expand Medicaid and protect and expand funding for mental health and substance abuse treatment. We need to keep an honest assessment of the drug and alcohol culture in Wyoming. The “Them and Us” delusion is not functional. Honesty is essential. Addiction is an endemic affliction of humanity. We should look for humane solutions.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: The race for Idaho’s top election official, the secretary of state, is a rematch
text:
"I Voted" stickers are available for voters to pick up after casting their ballot in the general election on Nov. 5, 2024, at Lowell Elementary School in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)In the race for Idaho’s top election official, two familiar names are headed to the ballot.
Democratic challenger Shawn Keenan is again challenging Republican incumbent Secretary of State Phil McGrane, who widely defeated Keenan in the 2022 election. 
Keenan, a mortgage broker and loan officer who lives in Coeur d’Alene, says he’s running again to avoid and combat election misinformation.
McGrane, a seasoned Idaho election official seeking a second term, says he’s running on a track record of keeping elections secure and improving access to election information. 
The two will be on the ballot in the Nov. 3 general election.
The secretary of state is a statewide office that oversees elections in the state, manages campaign finance compliance and transparency, and maintains records on businesses. The secretary of state also serves on the Land Board, which manages the state’s endowment lands.
The secretary of state serves a four-year term and earns an annual salary of $128,690.
In a Republican-controlled state, Keenan’s election bid faces tough odds. Voters in the state last elected a Democrat to statewide office in 2002, for the superintendent of public instruction. The state last had a Democratic secretary of state decades earlier. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Who is Shawn Keenan, the Democratic candidate for secretary of state?

Idaho Democratic candidate for secretary of state, Shawn Keenan. (Photo courtesy of Shawn Keenan)
Keenan, 49, has not worked in election administration but said he has been involved in politics from a young age and has worked on several Democratic campaigns in North Idaho. His parents moved to Idaho with him when he was 1 years old, he said. 
Keenan runs a nonprofit, called the North Idaho Kindness Project, that focuses on fostering acts of kindness — like love letters around Valentine’s Day and kindness tokens, which his group encourages people to hand out to people they see doing random acts of kindness. 
He said his initial bid for secretary of state four years ago came out of fear of growing distrust in election results — including among some of the then-Republican candidates for secretary of state. Years later, Keenan is still campaigning on that.
“When people start crafting these stories about elections not being secure or safe in Idaho, I wanted to be a voice for the truth: that they are indeed safe and secure and have been and always will be,” he said. 
Keenan praised McGrane, the incumbent, for his “due diligence.” And he said he and McGrane are on the same page on at least one policy priority: Establishing a state-issued voter guide, like other Western states have, that mails information on candidates and more directly to voters. 
As a Democrat in a reliably red state, he said he acknowledged that his odds of getting elected are tough — unless he puts in years of doorknocking. He said his campaign has largely focused on digital outreach to voters, compared to travel across the state.
With less than three weeks until the election, Keenan’s campaign has not raised any money, according to the state’s campaign finance database.
 Who is Phil McGrane, the Republican incumbent seeking a second term as secretary of state?

Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane (center) enters the House of Representative chambers to listen to Gov. Brad Little give his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
McGrane, 45, first started in election administration in Ada County in 2005 — years after a contentious recount of the George W. Bush v. Al Gore presidential election in Florida that brought concerns over partially hole punched “hanging chads.”
In the two decades since, he went to law school and worked in several areas of election administration — like operating voting equipment, training poll workers and entering voter registration cards into the state’s system. 
In 2018, McGrane was elected Ada County clerk. In 2022, he was elected as secretary of state, widely defeating Keenan with more than 72% of the vote.
McGrane said he’s proud of his work to improve access to election information — pointing to his office revamping a website that hosts resources for voters and candidates. The office also has updated the state’s campaign finance data dashboard and the state’s lobbying transparency website. 
“I’ve been working in elections my entire career. I think … the work I’ve done at Ada County, both in the elections team, but also as the elected clerk, and then here as Secretary of State, I think I’ve had a long history of making sure that voting is easy, that voting is secure, and that Idahoans can have confidence in their elections,” he said.
If re-elected, McGrane said his priorities would be to overhaul the state’s business registration system, update the state’s dated campaign finance laws, re-establish the presidential primary election and ask the Legislature for approval to create a voter guide with information on candidates
McGrane’s campaign has raised more than $440,000, and has about $171,000 in cash on hand, according to the state campaign finance database, which his office manages.
 How would the candidates approach running elections?

Keenan said the key difference between him and his opponent is the type of pressure they’d face from their political parties. 
“He does a good job of trying to hold the line when it comes to just the important work of delivering fair and safe elections,” Keenan said. “I don’t think I would have any — the same kind of party pressure to deal with that Phil (McGrane) has to.”
But Keenan reiterated an assurance he offered ahead of the 2022 general election: That the state would be OK if his opponent won.
“At the end of the day, I don’t feel like the office of secretary of state is being threatened by a candidate that is not capable of performing well for the citizens of Idaho,” Keenan said. “So I have full confidence, win or lose, that myself or Phil (McGrane) will be able to fulfill the necessary duties for the citizens of Idaho.”
But McGrane said he doesn’t see it as him working against partisan pressure. 
Even when he disagreed with the Idaho Republican Party — over regulations around closed primary elections — or the Trump administration when it comes to sensitive voter roll data, he said he’s maintained good relationships with them.
The same week that the U.S. Justice Department sued McGrane over refusing to turn over sensitive information in voter records to the Trump administration, McGrane said he was in the White House celebrating St. Patrick’s Day with President Donald Trump. 
And he said he talks frequently to Dorothy Moon, the chairwoman of the Idaho Republican Party, who McGrane narrowly defeated in the 2022 GOP primary election for secretary of state.
“It shows that it is not so simple as what people read in the news and the way things are framed in the news,” McGrane said. “That the best form of government — whether that’s state and federal government or it’s just here within the state, state officers, us with the Legislature — is government that works together and coordinates together. And that’s part of my leadership and something, if I have the good fortune of being reelected here and serving Idaho some more, I’m going to continue to work to pull people together — pull people together in the state of Idaho, and pull people together across the country.”
