name: Rhode Island Current
title: On Connecticut bear hunt, Gov. Lamont and GOP challenger Fazio find common ground
text:
A black bear tagged by the Connecticut Department of Energy and Environmental Protection to track the species' population. (Courtesy CT DEEP)This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.
When it comes to Connecticut’s increasingly troublesome relationship with black bears, both candidates in this year’s governor’s race are in agreement on a somewhat controversial solution.
Gov. Ned Lamont, the Democratic incumbent, and his opponent, Republican Sen. Ryan Fazio, have both supported measures in recent years to allow the hunting of black bears. Those efforts have been repeatedly defeated by opponents of hunting who argue that non-lethal means can be effective at reducing conflicts with people.
Connecticut is home to between 1,000 and 1,200 black bears, with the population concentrated largely in the state’s northwest corner. Encounters with people — including home break-ins and attacks on livestock — have risen in recent years, according to wildlife officials.
However, Connecticut is one of only two states in the Northeast that does not allow bear hunting. The other, Rhode Island, has fewer than a dozen bears. A Coventry, Rhode Island, resident recently posted a video of a bear walking onto her front steps and tearing at her home’s siding shingles, apparently trying to reach a wasp nest underneath the shingles.
The state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection, which tracks and helps manage the state’s bear population, has repeatedly sought support from lawmakers to establish a regulated hunting season, with Lamont’s backing. Lamont was also asked about the idea during a Democratic primary debate in July, saying he supported a hunt. His opponent in the primary, Rep. Josh Elliott of Hamden, said he was opposed.
“The governor supports a limited and carefully regulated bear hunt because Connecticut’s bear population is continuing to grow and we’re seeing more and more conflicts between bears and people every year,” Lamont campaign spokesperson Lauren Gray said in a statement. “Bears are now in all 169 towns, and residents are dealing with bears getting into homes, damaging property and threatening pets and livestock. We’ve tried education, prevention and other measures, and those efforts will continue, but the governor believes we also need to have additional tools available to manage the population and keep people safe.”
Gray added, “That doesn’t mean an unlimited hunt. Any hunt should be regulated and based on the best available science, with DEEP determining the appropriate limits.”
The most recent serious effort to enact a bear hunt came in 2025, when a bill dealing with the killing of nuisance bears was amended in the Senate to give the governor the ability to order DEEP to schedule a hunting season if the number of conflicts rise to a level that poses “a threat to public safety.” Fazio voted for the amended bill, which passed the chamber on a bipartisan vote of 34-2.
In the House, however, opponents amended the bill again in the final hours of the legislative session to remove the language permitting a hunt. The bill died upon returning to the Senate.
In an interview last week, Fazio said that having a “controlled and regulated bear hunt” is necessary to protect public safety. He specifically pointed to an incident in 2022, when a black bear attacked and injured a 12-year-old boy in Morris.
“We know the bear population is increasing at an unsustainable rate, especially in northwest and north-central and western Connecticut,” Fazio said. “Bears are smarter animals than most, and they have no fear of human beings because of our state policy currently.”
Fazio also criticized the governor’s lack of success in getting a bear hunting bill through the legislature, despite having a 2-1 majority of Democrats in both chambers.
“I think if you can’t get it done in eight years and you think it should get done, then you have a problem, and you deserve some criticism for it,” Fazio said.
In the absence of a hunt, DEEP has focused its efforts to reduce conflicts on a public awareness campaign encouraging residents to take steps such as removing bird feeders and keeping trash cans indoors between the spring and fall, when bears are most active.
In this July 25, 2014, file photo, a black bear in captivity awaits handouts at the the Maine Wildlife Park in Gray, Maine.
DEEP also hired a team of researchers from Mississippi State University this summer to conduct the first scientific survey of the state’s bear population in more than a decade. The results of that survey are expected to be released in the spring.
Sen. Christine Cohen, D-Guilford, a former chair of the legislature’s Environment Committee who has been an outspoken opponent of bear hunting, said state officials lack the data on bear population growth they’d need to determine whether a hunt is necessary. In the meantime, she said, more can be done to condition bears to avoid humans.
“I still contend that if the problem we’re trying to solve is bears coming into neighborhoods, which is what we hear over and over again, killing them doesn’t address the underlying cause — which is really the availability of human food,” Cohen said.
In 2023, Lamont signed a measure passed by lawmakers clarifying the circumstances in which bears may be killed in self-defense and allowing DEEP to issue permits to farmers whose crops or livestock were damaged by nuisance bears. The law also made it illegal to intentionally feed “potentially dangerous animals,” including bobcats, coyotes and bears.
DEEP has since issued 21 permits stemming from agricultural damage, resulting in the lawful killing of 36 bears.
The agency has also charged at least seven people with unauthorized killings of black bears since 2012. The majority of those cases involved claims of self-defense or defense of animals, according to a review published in CT Insider.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: DeSantis seeks ‘major disaster’ declaration from Trump post-Isaias
text:
A person walks through the wind and rain as Hurricane Isaias passes through Pensacola, Florida, on Oct. 9, 2026. The storm in the Gulf of Mexico is the season's first Atlantic hurricane. (Photo by Joe Raedle/Getty Images)Florida has asked for a major disaster declaration from the White House a week after Hurricane Isaias tore through a swath of the Panhandle and was blamed for six deaths.
Gov. Ron DeSantis announced Friday that state officials had made the request to the Federal Emergency Management Agency the night before — a step the governor noted would “unlock support” for federal reimbursements to local governments as well as aid to individuals dealing with damaged or destroyed homes and businesses.
“Look, you got to jump through bureaucratic hoops with this process. It’s just is what it is. And our folks did that very, very well. And so, that was submitted last night. They have it and we expect a decision on that very, very, quickly,” DeSantis said.
Cher Stanturf and her daughter Priscilla examine the damage to Cher’s home in the Welcome Mat trailer park on Oct. 10, 2026, the morning after Hurricane Isaias ripped through Pensacola, Florida. (Photo by Jay Waagmeester/Florida Phoenix)
To justify federal assistance, state and local officials generally must conduct a preliminary damage assessment of the magnitude of destruction and unmet needs of individuals, businesses, the public sector, and the community as a whole, according to federal regulations.
The governor didn’t share any of those details during a press conference in Milton, where he announced the request.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Division of Emergency Management, which submitted the request to FEMA, didn’t respond to the Phoenix’s request for the information.
Hurricane Isaias rose quickly out of the Gulf of Mexico and made landfall near Destin on Oct. 9 as a Category 2 storm. Initially, state officials worried about damage from storm surge but DeSantis has noted it was wind that had caused the most destruction, toppling trees and downing power lines.
The damage from Isaias, however, must be severe enough that the situation is “beyond the capability” of the state and local governments to absorb and that “supplemental federal emergency assistance is necessary to save lives and protect property, public health and safety, or to lessen or avert the threat of a disaster,” according to the FEMA website.
The 15 counties that could qualify for public assistance if approved by President Donald Trump are Bay, Calhoun, Escambia, Franklin, Gadsden, Gulf, Holmes, Jackson, Jefferson, Liberty, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Wakulla, Walton, and Washington.
People who experienced damage to their homes in the following eight counties could qualify for  individual assistance: Bay, Escambia, Gulf, Holmes, Okaloosa, Santa Rosa, Walton, and Washington.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC opens former utility workers’ retreat as 51st state park
text:
Ramsey Grove State Park, which features groves of live oak trees, is open to the public. (Photo courtesy of the Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism)South Carolina’s newest state park, which once served as a retreat for employees of a state utility, is open to the public.
Ramsey Grove State Park in Georgetown officially started welcoming visitors at the beginning of the month. During the “soft opening,” the park will open only from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. on weekdays, except for scheduled deer hunting days, according to the parks department.
A full opening date is not yet set.
SC parks department seeks $18M to open 4 new state parks

“We are thrilled to welcome visitors to Ramsey Grove State Park to experience the beauty and reverence of this special place,” said agency director Duane Parrish in a statement. “As we continue to plan for additional facilities and features, the soft opening allows the public to explore the trails, discover rich history, and gain a deeper understanding of the region’s cultural heritage.”
Admission is $8 for adults, $5 for seniors, $4 for children over the age of 5, and free for children 5 and under.
The 2,650-acre property, nestled against the Black River, includes 7 miles of hiking trails and is a popular site for birdwatching, according to the parks department.
The site started as a plantation in 1731. In 1850, nearly 400 slaves farmed rice on the land. A hunting lodge with portions built as early as the 1770s still stands among the oak groves.
Most recently, the land was a retreat for staff of SCANA, the former utility company that oversaw the failed V.C. Summer nuclear power plant. After buying SCANA in 2019, Dominion Energy agreed to donate four properties to the state. That 2021 deal was part of a settlement meant to offset roughly $165 million the utility owed in unpaid taxes that would have been forgiven if the nuclear plant had been completed.
One of the properties, Bundrick Island on Lexington County’s Lake Murray, went to the Department of Natural Resources. Also known as Sandy Beach, it’s accessible only by boat.
The parks department received Ramsey Grove, along with Pine Island in Lexington County and Misty Lake in Aiken County.
A hunting lodge, portions of which date back to the 1770s, sits in Ramsey Grove State Park in Georgetown, S.C. (Photo courtesy of SC Department of Parks, Recreation and Tourism)
Pine Island State Park opened to the public in October 2025. Misty Lake does not yet have an opening date.
Ramsey Grove is the 51st state park.
After opening two parks in two decades, Ramsey Grove marks the third park to open in the past two years, with at least three more in the works, a boom caused in part by the donations from Dominion Energy.
Legislators spent $15 million on developing those prospective parks last year, including establishing hiking trails and repairing buildings, on top of $10 million during the two years before that.
The state agency recommends checking the park’s website before heading out. Scheduled closures for hunting include every weekend in October.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Losing bidder claims state changed terms on I-24 toll lane project
text:
A transportation consortium that lost a bid to build toll lanes on 1-24 from Nashville to Murfreesboro is suing the state. (Photo: John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)A road-building group that lost out on Tennessee’s toll lane project is challenging the state’s award to a consortium led by a Spain-based company that promised the state a massive amount of money.
A group of companies called 24 Choice Lanes Partners says in the filing the Tennessee Department of Transportation gave its competitor an edge by allowing it to change the terms of a record-setting payout after bidding took place.
The group filed a petition Thursday in Davidson County Chancery Court requesting a review of the Tennessee Department of Transportation decision to award the I-24 toll lanes project to DriveTN, a group that guaranteed it would give the state more than $24 billion to land the contract for a $9.2 billion project.
24 Choice Lanes Partners says the state selected DriveTN, which is headed by the Spanish company Ferrovial, “based on an outlier financial proposal that TDOT knew, or through its own post-selection diligence should have known, could not be carried through to contract on the terms offered.”
The group says the state’s “subsequent error” in entering a final agreement on the $24.8 billion payment deviates from DriveTN’s first payment terms in which it promised to pay the state within seven years of closing the deal. 
24 Choice Lanes Partners and another group both promised to pay the state around $7 billion to take on the project, which runs from southeast Nashville to Murfreesboro.
The plaintiff says the state is allowing DriveTN to “reduce, defer or stretch those payments far beyond the construction period,” of seven years, according to the filing. “Any change to the payment amount or timing of payment proposed and evaluated in the DriveTN proposal is material — and prohibited.”
The group challenging the bid furthers its argument by saying DriveTn received an advantage over other bidders.
24 Choice Lanes Partners says TDOT disclosed every competitor’s financial proposals at a public meeting, then made their financial offers available for review by DriveTN before executing the “concession” agreement, giving the winning consortium the opportunity to renegotiate its financial terms knowing “exactly how far it could cut its commitments and still sit above the field.”
In contrast, other bidders made their offers “blind” and were held to it, the filing says.
The filing adds that the process “strikes at the integrity of the procurement and undermines any competition” that might have existed. 
Asked if the state was concerned about a potential challenge before the lawsuit was filed, a Transportation Department spokesperson told the Lookout the Transportation Modernization Act does not include a protest provision for P3 procurements.
Lawmakers passed the act in 2023 to allow for a public-private toll lane project and setting up the board that awarded the bid to DriveTN. It also approved $3.3 billion from the state’s general fund for road projects.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ACLU of New Mexico sues ICE over detention contract documents
text:
The American Civil Liberties Union of New Mexico on Oct. 16, 2026, announced it had filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency over outstanding public records request related to detention contracts in the state at Cibola and Torrance counties' detention facilities (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM).The American Civil Liberties Union of New Mexico on Friday announced it had filed a federal lawsuit against the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency over outstanding public records request related to detention contracts in the state.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In a news release, ACLU-NM said it filed the suit in federal court on behalf of the New Mexico Immigrant Law Center, which has outstanding Freedom of Information Act requests with the agency for records of ICE’s contracting agreements with CoreCivic, which runs the Torrance County Detention Facility and Cibola County Correctional Center.
State lawmakers passed and Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham earlier this year signed into law the Immigrant Safety Act, House Bill 9, which prohibits local governments across the state from signing detention contracts with ICE.
The U.S. Justice Department sued the state over the law in May. That case remains pending, according to the most recent court docket update.
“We’re concerned that ICE just replaced one underhanded contract with another,” Emma O’Sullivan, staff attorney at the ACLU of New Mexico, said in a statement. “The state made it clear with the passage of the Immigrant Safety Act that New Mexico stands against the mistreatment and abuse of people in these detention facilities. ICE cannot continue to operate here without accountability.”
In March, the ACLU noted, ICE announced non-competitive “sole source” direct contracts with CoreCivic in both Torrance and Cibola counties to continue detaining immigrants there. “ICE sidestepped important federal contracting requirements that generally require competitive bidding and a review of contractors’ safety records,” the ACLU news release said, noting little information is available about the contracts.
Source NM has a pending request with ICE for comment.
“Our communities spoke up and passed the Immigrant Safety Act to say that we refuse to be complicit in locking up immigrants, yet ICE is doing everything in its power to retain and expand Trump’s cruel detention and deportation machine in our state,” Jessica I. Martínez, director of policy and coalition building at NMILC, said in a statement. “We’re requesting these documents because New Mexicans deserve to know why ICE and the Trump administration are attempting to evade our laws while they continue to subject people to inhumane detention.”
The ACLU news release also noted ongoing concerns about health and safety at the detention facilities in the state.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Colorado to receive federal funding to support Aspen Acres Fire recovery
text:
An image smoke coming from the Aspen Acres Fire posted on July 2, 2026. (Courtesy of Aspen Acres Fire 2026 Facebook)The U.S. Small Business Administration has approved Colorado’s request for funding to support businesses harmed by a wildfire that grew to over 100,000 acres in southern Colorado this summer. 
The Aspen Acres Fire, the seventh-largest wildfire in Colorado history, destroyed more than 200 structures across Pueblo and Custer counties. 
Loans will be available for businesses to repair or replace damaged property and meet financial obligations that cannot be met as a result of the fire. Homeowners and renters can also apply for loans to repair or replace property damaged by the fire. Funds can also be used to protect property from future damage that may come up as a result of damage from the fire.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Starting Monday, the Small Business Administration will open Disaster Loan Assistance Centers in Pueblo and Custer counties where residents, property owners, renters, nonprofits and business owners can seek assistance applying for loans.
Loans are also available to support businesses who suffered economic injury in counties surrounding the fire: Crowley, El Paso, Fremont, Huerfano, Las Animas, Lincoln, Otero and Saguache counties.
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis issued a major disaster declaration for the fire, opening up more state resources as well as Federal Emergency Management Agency funding to support firefighting efforts. President Donald Trump approved public assistance funding for communities harmed by the fire, but denied individual assistance and hazard mitigation funding. 
State officials announced earlier this week that an investigation had determined the fire was ignited by an aspen tree that fell on a power line during high winds at the end of June. The fire is 82% contained, more than three months after it started.  
Colorado recently saw several requests for federal disaster support denied amid Trump administration’s targeting of Colorado. Trump promised “harsh measures” if the state did not release election denier and former Republican Mesa County Clerk Tina Peters from prison. An email revealed in court proceedings showed that an administration official, hours before Trump renewed his public calls for Peters’ release last December, summoned federal agencies to talk about “immediate actions that your department or agency can take with respect to Colorado.”
The administration denied Colorado FEMA recovery funding for the Elk and Lee fires in April. 
Polis commuted Peters’ prison sentence, and the Colorado Department of Corrections released her in June. She has since repeatedly met with the president.
Polis declared a statewide drought emergency in Colorado in June with “severe” or “extreme” drought conditions across the state. 
Climate change has led to increased wildfire risk in Colorado since much of the state has grown hotter and drier in recent decades. The three largest wildfires in Colorado history all occurred in 2020.

name: VTDigger
title: Rural Vermont is losing its say over its own land
text:
This commentary is by Loralee Tester, executive director of the Northeast Kingdom Chamber of Commerce.
In 1989, the Galick family sold its farm in West Haven to The Nature Conservancy. The family believed this well-established organization would protect the generations of labor they had given to the land they loved.
The conservancy now plans to demolish it. The farmhouse, cow barn, creamery, sheep barn and machine shop are all slated to be torn down, even though some of the buildings date back to 1850. 
The conservancy knew what it had. It requested a barn preservation grant in 1997, at which time the farm was listed on the State Register of Historic Places. The conservancy then went to Vermont taxpayers for help. It accepted a state barn grant for the dairy barn in 2001, another for the field barn and a grant for the farmhouse in 2007. 
So the conservancy did not neglect these buildings in the beginning. It invested in them and asked the public to invest in them. The organization has told me it has no other option but to remove the buildings now, and that may very well be true. However, as any homeowner can attest, if routine maintenance isn’t conducted, a property will ultimately reach the point of no return. The real question is why it stopped maintaining a property it asked the public to help preserve. 

READ MORE

The Nature Conservancy reports roughly $10 billion in total assets. Last year it paid a single fundraising firm $11 million, and its chief executive officer earns close to $1 million. I run a small nonprofit in the Northeast Kingdom, and I work with businesses large and small that manage to fulfill their missions on tight budgets. An organization with $10 billion in assets can afford building maintenance. 
I don’t think this is a one-time situation. It’s a predictable result of how Vermont has chosen to define conservation. 
In 2023, the Legislature passed Act 59, which set a goal of conserving 30% of Vermont by 2030 and 50% by 2050. Under the law, land qualifies only if it’s permanently protected through deed restrictions, a conservation easement or outright purchase. That excludes roughly 2.5 million acres enrolled in Vermont’s Current Use program, which are all the working farms and managed forests that make up so much of this state. Leaving the program comes with a penalty, and in my experience, very few landowners opt to do so. 
The current inventory shows that 27% of Vermont is conserved; however, when land in the Current Use program is included, the figure is closer to 70% by my calculation. Vermonters have been conserving land all along; we simply are not giving them credit for it.
Meanwhile, the people doing that work are going under. In 2016, Vermont had 838 dairy farms. As of early this year, there were 414, and four processing plants are closing in 2026. Dairy keeps more than half of our farmland open — the fields and red barns on most of the tourism brochures that come through my office. Visitors spent $4.2 billion here in 2024, and they came, in part, for the working landscape. We are selling the view while the farmers who maintain it are losing their farms. 
Who is actually gaining from this current definition? The land that counts toward Act 59 is held through easements and acquisitions that large conservation organizations hold and raise money around. Several of those groups pushed hard for this bill. The Nature Conservancy, the Vermont Land Trust, Audubon Vermont and the Vermont Natural Resources Council all testified in support, and together they reported hundreds of thousands of dollars in lobbying spending during the 2023-24 biennium. Yes, this is how the system works, and there is nothing illegal about it, but what is happening is that organizations with paid staff are the ones that are shaping the policies that define our state, while the farmers, loggers, selectboard members and small-business owners are busy keeping the economy running and counting on our government to do what is right. 
I keep coming back to the question of what this policy is intended to accomplish that we are not already doing. And who is Vermont for? I’d like to say it’s for anyone who wants to make a life here, but right now it’s becoming harder and harder. 
There is no one I know in this state who is against conservation. It’s part of why we live where we do, and this region is what it is, not because of Act 250, but because the culture of working lands that defines rural Vermont has been created and maintained by those of us who make our lives here. It is becoming almost impossible to make the economics work anymore, and policies like Act 59 will continue to create disparities, inequities and unaffordability. Vermont is not only here to be a park for visitors. It is a beautiful state where many of us still want to have a chance at a prosperous and peaceful life. Remove the people, and you’re conserving an idea of Vermont that no one is left to maintain.
Beware of policies that affect entire regions without getting their buy-in. Consider for a moment whose voices are helping to craft those policies, and ask how it will affect all of us: our children and the future generations who feel that they need to leave in order to have a chance at a successful life. 
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Rural Vermont is losing its say over its own land.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico residents fighting to save solar observatory from demolition hail partial win
text:
The Sunspot Solar Observatory, pictured in 2022, faces demolition after liquid mercury leaked from the main telescope. (Courtesy of New Mexico State University and Josh Bachman)A coalition of New Mexico residents who spent the summer pushing to save a remote solar observatory from demolition are celebrating a partial victory.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Earlier this year, the National Science Foundation announced plans to demolish the nearly 80-year-old Sunspot Solar Observatory in the Sacramento Mountains near Alamogordo due to a liquid mercury leak inside the site’s aging telescope. A band of former employees, residents and even some state lawmakers quickly pushed back and asked NSF leaders to refrain from demolishing other facilities on the property, such as the visitor’s center, that could still be used or could be repurposed into educational attractions.
The coalition, known as Friends of Sunspot, has traveled southern New Mexico, seeking support from local city councils and elected leaders. Over the summer, Spaceport America’s executive director and the New Mexico House of Representatives majority whip backed their cause.
Their efforts quickly caught the attention of enthusiasts far outside New Mexico’s borders, too.
Rick St. Hilaire, a New Hampshire-based attorney and amateur solar observer, in September lodged a formal objection to the demolition with the NSF. In it, he wrote that he learned about the demolition plans as he sat down to plan a possible November trip to Sunspot.
“The treatment of these historic properties warrants reconsideration before irreversible demolition occurs,” St. Hilaire, who declined to discuss his involvement in greater detail with Source NM, wrote to NSF officials. “I ask that NSF not irreversibly destroy this nationally significant historic complex without the kind of reasoned decision-making that the Administrative Procedure Act sets as a standard.”
NSF Chief Officer for Research Facilities Linnea Avallone wrote back to him on Sept. 24, saying that she had contacted New Mexico State Historic Preservation Officer Michelle Ensey, whom she said understood “demolition of the Dunn Solar Telescope must proceed in order to remediate the mercury contamination.”
However, Avallone added that Ensey requested that NSF “clarify that the remainder of the historic properties at the site are not slated for demolition this Fall.” Avallone added that residents and other stakeholders will have a chance to lodge objections “before any demolition beyond that required for mercury remediation occurs.”
Stephen Hamway, a spokesperson for the New Mexico Historic Preservation Division, in an email to Source NM said that “it is NMHPD’s understanding that the demolition of the remaining historic facilities on the site may not happen this year, but is currently slated to take place sometime in 2027.”
The Sunspot Astronomy and Visitor’s Center, pictured in 2022. (Courtesy of New Mexico State University and Josh Bachman)
In social media groups dedicated to preserving historical observatories, posts describing the interaction between St. Hilaire and Avallone quickly spread as cause for optimism.
While many hailed the interaction as a pause on demolition, an NSF spokesperson disputed that characterization in a statement to Source NM.
“NSF’s plans have not changed: the agency still intends to demolish the remaining facilities at the site,” spokesperson Cassandra Eichner said in an email, adding that the agency is allowing objections to be heard out “before any further demolition occurs.”
Eichner added that the U.S. Forest Service is in contact with area stakeholders about potential future uses for the site and advised anyone with ideas to email them to ReImagineSunspotNM@usda.gov.
Dave Dooling, Sunspot’s former education officer who is now leading the local effort to stop demolition, told Source NM he believed St. Hilaire’s objection bought preservation advocates some much-needed time.
“We’re starting to get a little more traction,” he said. “It’s not a pause so much as it is further down the schedule. But that gives us some time to try and get it saved.”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: University of Iowa receives foundation grant for business student wellness initiative
text:
The University of Iowa Tippie College of Business received a $3.5 million grant to sustain its student mental health and wellness initiative. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)A multimillion-dollar donation to the University of Iowa’s business college, alongside a matching gift challenge to generate even more funds, will help support a student mental health and success initiative that sees participation from thousands.
The UI Tippie College of Business announced in a news release it has received $3.5 million from the DeWolf Family Foundation of Cedar Rapids for Tippie Thrive, a “peer-led” mental health program embedded in courses and with outside programming.
According to the release, the donation, and a 2-to-1 matching gift challenge with a commitment from the foundation that reaches $500,000, will establish an endowment for the initiative’s future and fund a “dedicated home and student-facing storefront” for Tippie Thrive.
“Tippie Thrive reflects our belief that student success requires more than academic achievement alone,” said business college dean Amy Kristof-Brown in the release. “Business leaders consistently tell us they need graduates who can collaborate effectively, navigate uncertainty, and lead with empathy and self-awareness. Tippie Thrive helps students develop those capabilities while supporting their personal well-being. We are deeply grateful to Chris and Suzy DeWolf for their extraordinary investment in our students and their future.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: FBI arrests CT man accused of threatening Republicans
text:
Connecticut’s political world ended the week with stark reminders of how political discourse has turned threatening: The state’s two Democratic U.S. senators were intended recipients of packages with substances that raised suspicions, and a Naugatuck man was arrested by the FBI and accused of threatening to kill Republicans.
Scott Dyer, 35, was charged with making interstate threats related to what federal authorities said were comments posted on YouTube, including, “I’m prepared to kill Republicans. Eager to do it actually. I already have targets in my local community selected.”
The comments were posted on Oct. 8 and 9. The U.S. attorney’s office announced his arrest Thursday.
“Threats of violence, whether tied to politics or any other motive, have no place on the internet or anywhere else in our society,” said David X. Sullivan, the U.S. attorney. “We will investigate these crimes quickly and prosecute those involved to deter this behavior, neutralize any threats and ensure the safety of the public.”
Dyer mentioned at least one Republican official in his threats, the U.S. attorney’s office said. It did not identify the person.
“I have a lot of hollow points with his name on if we ever get the chance to meet,” Dyer said, according to the federal charging documents. Dyer was released on $100,000 bond and placed in home confinement under electronic monitoring.
U.S. Sen. Chris Murphy told reporters Friday after a campaign event that his office had not yet been informed what the substance was that was mailed to his office.
Authorities intercepted the letter addressed to Murphy’s Hartford office and told congressional staffs to be vigilant. A staffer in U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal’s office set aside a letter deemed suspicious and alerted Hartford police.
“We’ve implemented new measures in our office, as have other congressional offices, to be a lot more careful about how we deal with the mail,” Murphy said. “There are some unhinged people out there with some pretty crazy conspiracy theories, and so we’re going to be vigilant, especially between now and the election.”

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Oklahoma treasurer’s race pits veteran against newcomer
text:
Treasurer's Office inside the Oklahoma State Capitol Building (Photo by Kyle Phillips/For Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – The race for state treasurer pits a government finance expert against a political newcomer who says he does not expect to win.
State Auditor and Inspector Cindy Byrd, a Republican, faces Libertarian Kiefer Perry on the Nov. 3 ballot.
“I probably know more about the finances of Oklahoma, both at the state and local government, than most officials serving,” said Byrd, who is term limited as state auditor.
Oklahoma State Auditor and Inspector Cindy Byrd presents an audit of state agency compliance in spending federal dollars at the state Capitol on Aug. 27, 2025. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)
Byrd easily defeated Republican incumbent State Treasurer Todd Russ in the June 26 primary with nearly 62% of the vote.
Byrd initially announced she was running for lieutenant governor but switched to treasurer after President Donald Trump endorsed T.W. Shannon in that race.
She said the endorsement made her pause to consider what she really wanted to do. 
On Oct. 1, Trump endorsed Byrd for state treasurer during a rally in Durant.
Byrd, 53, said she was grateful for the endorsement but never believed an endorsement put someone over the top when it comes to winning an election.
Byrd, of Coalgate, has worked for the state auditor’s office for nearly 30 years, the last eight as state auditor and inspector.
Despite the vast difference in experience and name recognition, Byrd said she is not taking anything for granted.
“I don’t leave anything to chance,” she said.
Perry, 37, of Broken Arrow, works at Lowe’s changing out displays and fixtures.
Kiefer Perry (Provided photo)
It is the first time he has run for elected office.
He decided to run so that Libertarians would maintain ballot access.
“We didn’t have as many people running for offices this year, and so I volunteered at our last state convention that I would put my name in the hat, so to speak, to try to gather the required votes needed to retain ballot access for future elections,” Perry said.
For Libertarians to continue to be recognized, one of their candidates for statewide office must receive 2.5% of the total votes cast for the office in either of the two preceding general elections, according to the State Election Board website.
“Looking at our past record in these kinds of races our candidates received in excess of 20 percent,” said Chris Powell, past chairperson of the Oklahoma Libertarian Party.
Perry said that although he does not expect to win, he wants to use the opportunity to spread the Libertarian message of limited government and provide options to voters.
He wants to protect the personal rights and freedoms of individuals, he said.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Special committee identifies improvements for state-run Mt. Edgecumbe High School
text:
Mt. Edgecumbe High School, a state-run boarding school serving grades 9 through 12, is seen in Sitka on Oct. 6, 2025 (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)Clear communication at the state-run boarding school Mt. Edgecumbe High School is among the top priority areas to improve students’ residential and academic life, a special committee told members of the Alaska State Board of Education this week.
The state board established the committee last March to review concerns and create recommendations for improvements after a tumultuous school year at Mt. Edgecumbe. Challenges included state budget cuts, staff and administrative turnover, and a wave of student disenrollment. In the 2025-2026 school year, nearly 100 students, a quarter of the student population, left the school.
The disenrollments put Mt. Edgecumbe in the spotlight, prompting legislative hearings, an investigatory visit from Alaska senators and representatives and questions about deteriorating facilities and reductions in staffing, students activities and support services, as well as concerns around students’ mental health and quality of life.     

Mt. Edgecumbe Superintendent David Langford (left) and Deena Bishop, commissioner of the Alaska Department of Education and Early Development are seen on Feb. 11, 2026. They testified before several committees of lawmakers on the conditions at the boarding school, after over 100 students disenrolled. (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

The Alaska Department of Education and Early Development administers the school with the governor-appointed Board of Education. The school’s population is predominantly Alaska Native students from across the state. Deena Bishop, the state’s education commissioner, told lawmakers in February that the rapid changes at the school were part of a “right-sizing” effort after COVID pandemic relief funding ran out in 2024, forcing the high school into a series of cost-cutting measures in 2025.
Legislators responded this year, approving millions for repairs and renovations to dorms, classrooms and dining facilities, and $450,000 for student travel, utilities costs, student activities and mental health services this school year. 
Kadyn Cross, a junior and student body president at Mt Edgecumbe, is from the village of Koyuk on the coast of Norton Sound. He participated in the special committee and told the board on Wednesday that while progress has been made, money only goes so far. 
“I’ve seen facilities fall into despair, leaky ceilings, outdated dorms and a cafeteria that struggled to meet basic expectations. I’ve also seen students and staff leave because they lost faith in the school and the system,” he said. 
“But this year things are looking up. Legislature approved millions in funding for repairs,” he said. “There’s a new system of sense of optimism on our campus, and I would like to say that trust will not be rebuilt by money alone. It will be rebuilt by transparency, communication and by a clear understanding of who is responsible for what.”
Clear and consistent communication among students, families, teachers, staff and administrators was a major theme of the 22 recommendations developed by the committee. 
The committee consisted of two students, two parents, a tribal representative, an alumni, and a member of the Mt. Edgecumbe advisory board and a state board member. They conducted surveys with 186 students, 65 parents and 14 staff to collect input and identified recommendations across five categories: school culture, student engagement, communication, academics and student life. 
Students and families want timely information from Mt. Edgecumbe on school matters, the committee said, and changes in protocols, including dormitory policies and expectations, academics, and on and off-campus activities. It also noted communication with families should take into account potential limitations of reaching families in rural Alaska, as students attend from over 100 communities across the state.     

Paul Reid, with the Office of Education Advocacy with the Alaska Department of Education and Early Development (left) presents the special ad hoc committee’s recommendations for Mt. Edgecumbe to the state Board of Education at their fall meeting in Sitka on Oct. 14, 2026. (Photo by Anna Laffrey)
 

The committee recommended the school should establish appropriate channels for students to provide feedback on rules, policies and procedures that affect their experience, especially around the student dorms and when changes are under consideration. It emphasized the administration should continue to improve the quality and conditions of the student dorms, and increase responsiveness to “long-standing and intermittent” maintenance concerns.
Recommendations included strengthening support for students, with a more proactive approach to addressing mental health and wellbeing, including clear roles and responsibilities for staff. The committee advised developing more peer-mentoring among upperclassmen and younger students to bolster school culture and engagement.
It also advised establishing a process for surveying students and families that withdraw from Mt. Edgecumbe in order to identify and address concerns and improve student retention.
On the academic side, the committee recommended an increased focus on preparing students for life after graduation, with clear grade-level progression of expectations, resources and opportunities to boost readiness for college, career training and the workforce. It also advised more opportunities for parent involvement in academic planning.
Following the presentation of recommendations to the state board on Wednesday, Board of Education Chair Sally Stockhausen said she wants to see updates from DEED and the administration on the work completed and progress in each category. 
“I would like it to stay in the forefront of our minds and not become another thing that we put on the shelf — ‘Well, that was nice that we did that,’” she said. “And so I would like to see, in a format that addresses these recommendations at our meetings, that we get a regular update on what has been done so far… both from the admin and staff perspective, but then also from the student perspective. I think we need to keep their voice very much in this the whole time.”
Upgrades and improvements underway
The Board of Education held its meeting in person at Mt. Edgecumbe in Sitka this week, which included a tour of the campus and meetings with students and staff. On Wednesday, Superintendent David Langford gave a presentation to board members further detailing the significant upgrades in progress across the campus. 
“It’s amazing what can happen in a single year,” said Langford, who was hired in July 2025.     

Mt Edgecumbe High School student dormitories are seen on Oct. 6, 2025 (Photo by Corinne Smith/Alaska Beacon)
 

Langford said $24 million in additional state funds is earmarked for upgrades and renovations over the next several years. That includes a complete kitchen and cafeteria renovation and replacing leaky dorm windows and roofs. He said already the administration has made upgrades to the food served in the cafeteria and the dorms, including new dorm furniture and replacing decades-old laundry machines and mattresses — which was of particular concern for legislators during their visit. 
“We even threw out about 60 mattresses that were here from World War II that were in our storage. We weren’t actually using them, but we discovered them and got rid of them,” he said. “So thankfully, thanks to our legislature, all the mattresses have now been upgraded.”
Langford said this year Mt. Edgecumbe is fully staffed academically. He said all students have access to new computers thanks to a grant from the Alaska Federation of Natives. He said staff has made upgrades to classrooms and teacher and staff training —  and English curriculum, which is the first update in roughly a decade, he noted. 
“Nobody could even remember the last time they got a new curriculum. So, thanks to the support of DEED and the reading program, we were able to get the first (new) curriculum in 10 years. And just two days ago, the books arrived, so we’re very excited about that,” he said.
He said the school is still working on hiring a full-time mental health clinician, but has a wellness coordinator on staff and has contracted local counselors. Langford said this year new opportunities for extra-curricular activities, trips to town, sports and Alaska Native cultural activities have grown. 
Despite the attention and improvements, enrollment is still down this year. As of Oct. 1, there were 350 students enrolled, down from an average of roughly 400 students, but enrollment is still in flux, Langford said. 
During public testimony, Mt. Edgecumbe alumni, parents and current and former staff emphasized the need for continued support and investment from the board, DEED and the administration for the future of the school. Xander Swanson, a student government representative, highlighted the school’s unique culture and education for students from across the state.
“We are the only place where students from the Arctic, the Interior, the Aleutians, the Yukon-Kuskokwim and the Southeast live together, learn together and become one community. We bring our languages, our traditions and our home communities with us and share them,” he said. “And when we graduate, we don’t stay here. We go back, or we go on, and we carry what we learn to our villages, our regions, and the state. It has been true for generations. Our job is to make sure that stays true. Thank you for investing in us.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Rebecca Bennett outraises Tom Kean Jr., but Kean holds cash edge
text:
Rebecca Bennett (D) and Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) are competing in the closely watched House race in New Jersey’s 7th District. (Photos by Anne-Marie Caruso/Hal Brown)[2026 election Voter Guide: Who is running in this November’s midterm elections?]In the most closely watched House race in the state, Democratic Rebecca Bennett outraised Rep. Tom Kean Jr. (R) more than 4-to-1 in the most recent quarter, but a slower burn rate and reserves Kean built in 2025 still lend the incumbent a cash edge in the race’s final days.
Bennett, who is hoping to oust the two-term incumbent in New Jersey’s 7th Congressional District, reported raising about $3.9 million between July 1 and Sept. 30 in a quarterly filing to the Federal Election Commission. That total trounced the $974,612 Kean reported bringing in over the same period.
Though Kean’s fundraising lagged that of his opponent, Kean’s third-quarter haul still represents an increase from prior quarters, when a prolonged absence kept his fundraising down. Kean said he was being treated for depression during this time.
Democrat Rebecca Bennett campaigns with Gabby Giffords in push to flip House seat

The latest figures leave Bennett’s cycle-wide fundraising significantly higher than Kean’s. The former U.S. Navy helicopter pilot has raised around $8.2 million this cycle, to the incumbent’s $5.9 million.
But Bennet has consistently spent more money and faster. That trend continued in the third quarter, when Bennett’s campaign poured more than $3.6 million into the contest.
Kean spent only $2.3 million that quarter, and his spending for the cycle totaled less than $3.8 million, to Bennett’s less than $6.5 million.
He entered the final month of the race with more money banked. He reported a little under $2.3 million in reserves, compared to the roughly $1.7 million Bennett had.
Kean, a former state lawmaker, was first elected to Congress in 2022, flipping the seat for the GOP. His campaign for reelection has dinged Bennett for her ties to a hospital system that has been flagged for poor quality control and denial of care. Democrats have attacked Kean for missing votes in Congress during his absence earlier this year.
Though Bennet has consistently outraised Kean, the incumbent has benefitted far more from outside spending than his opponent.
The congressman has seen at least $4.8 million in independent expenditures boosting him or dinging Bennett. The overwhelming share of that money came in the form of ad buys from Land I Love PAC.
The group was funded with nearly $4.2 million from the Congressional Leadership Fund, House Republicans’ super PAC, and poured about that much money into media placements in the district before the fund pulled support for Kean earlier this month.
He’s also been the beneficiary of $460,408 in digital ads and mailers from Elon Musk’s America PAC, $38,976 in digital ads from the Trump-aligned super PAC Maga Inc., and $160,576 in text messaging from No Going Back PAC, another Trump-aligned group.
Bennett’s outside support has been far slimmer.
The Battleground Alliance PAC put $156,810 behind canvassing in the 7th District. The Progressive Turnout Project and Growing Economic Opportunities, a PAC with ties to laborers’ unions, have put $129,502 and $16,334 in for canvassing to boost Bennett.
American Bridge 21st Century has spent $174,708 on billboards and other media boosting Bennett.
Election Day is Nov. 3.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: ‘We’ve got to button it up’: Childcare council reduces schedule, shifts priorities ahead of session
text:
Shannon Tremblay (left), director of the New Hampshire Child Care Advisory Council, and Marianne Barter, the council's former chair, sit during a meeting of the council on Aug. 14, 2025. (Photo by Claire Sullivan/New Hampshire Bulletin)The New Hampshire Child Care Advisory Council is reducing the number of its scheduled meetings ahead of a new legislative session and another budget year. 
The council was legislatively enacted in 1995 and serves as the official advisory body for childcare matters in New Hampshire. The council’s role is to inform and advise the Department of Health and Human Services, the governor, the state Legislature, and the Department of Education on early education and childcare policy.  
At the council’s annual meeting on Oct. 8, members voted to reduce the meeting schedule from every other month to quarterly to give members “more time for meaningful discussion and decisions on complex issues.” 
“Meetings were getting to be where it was more of just an update meeting, and not actually like getting any real good work done as far as making recommendations to either legislators or state level,” said Shannon Tremblay, director of the council. “So the recommendation came to start meeting quarterly and have those meetings be a little bit longer and not so many updates.” 
The council comprises voting members who represent early education organizations, the state’s childcare resource and referral network, the business community, the state community college system, the state university system and governor-appointed “consumers of childcare services.” 
In addition to reducing the frequency of meetings, the vote also changed the length and scope. The two-hour meetings will now be three to four hours with a “stricter” agenda in hopes that council members and presenters prioritize policy initiatives instead of providing updates. 
“We’ve got to button it up,” said Marianne Barter, executive director of Merrimack Valley Day Care Center in Concord and formal council chair. 
 The change comes as childcare advocates prepare for a new legislative session and budget year. While the council is nonpartisan, meetings have been a place where advocates, providers and council members align on priorities for the year ahead. 
In preparation, meetings will also have topics of discussion “aligned to the work” and the state legislative cycle. Advocates have stated they try to renew momentum for state dollars to go toward the childcare workforce grant, childcare quality funding and out-of-school-time program. 
As director, Tremblay holds the only paid position on the council and is responsible for managing its affairs. She said the “bulk” of work of the council does not happen at advisory meetings, and reducing the commitment will make it easier for members to get things done. 
“There still will be time for those updates because we’re going to have a longer meeting, but have more space for discussion about what’s happening around,” Tremblay said.  
Council meetings will now be reserved for deliberation, decision and statutory advisory work, while provider input, workgroup preparation and updates will happen between meetings. 
Despite more work being done offline, Tremblay said the council will still be “very transparent.” State law requires that representatives from the Department of Health and Human Services on behalf of the commissioner and the Bureau of Child Development and Head Start Collaboration attend. It is one of the few times childcare providers can publicly hear from state officials that manage childcare governance regarding policy changes and updates, as well as voice their concerns to the people directly responsible for implementing them. 
“It’s not necessarily like we’re trying to go behind closed doors,” she said. “There’s so much stuff going on and things happening everywhere. We’re really trying to focus on policy and making sure that providers are getting the information.” 
Under the new schedule, the next council meeting is planned for Jan. 14.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi has its own history book of ‘Laughter and Forgetting,’ professor writes
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi Today Ideas is a platform for thoughtful ideas to be shared about our state’s past, present and future. Opinions expressed in guest essays are the author’s own and do not necessarily represent those of Mississippi Today. You can read more about the section here.  

At first it might appear that modern-day Mississippi has nothing in common with the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic of 1952. Red-state free-market conservatism versus a dictatorship of the proletariat? Tate Reeves versus Stalinist fellow-travelers? But metaphor and human sociopolitical behavior being what they are, there’s a connection. Let me explain. 
In February of 1948, the Czechoslovakian Communist Party seized power in a coup-d’etat. On Feb. 21, the party chairman, Klement Gottwald, addressed a celebratory crowd in Prague’s Old-Town Square. To his right stood another high-ranking Communist official, Vladimír Clementis. It was bitterly cold and Clementis thoughtfully placed his fur hat on comrade Gottwald’s bare head. Photographs of the occasion were distributed by the state, with the dour Communist power couple gazing out on the citizens and bright future of the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic. 
Gottwald became Prime Minister, while Clementis was appointed minister of foreign affairs. But authoritarian power dynamics being what they are, Clementis’ position and gracious gesture toward Gottwald did not guarantee his safety. (Are you listening, Marco Rubio?)
In 1952 Clementis was arrested and charged with being a “bourgeois nationalist,” which in Stalin’s world was usually fatal. During the requisite show trial, Clementis confessed to his “crimes” and was later hanged. Because Clementis had become a persona non grata, the state propaganda apparatus removed his face from the 1948 photograph with Gottwald, shifting most of Clementis’ head to hidden behind a microphone. The only identifiable part of Clementis that remained was his fur hat, still perched atop Gottwald’s head.

On the left, the original photograph from Feb. 21, 1948. Klement Gottwald is on the right, while Vladimír Clementis is to the left, partially obscured by the microphone. In the retouched photograph on the right, Clementis’ head is hidden by the microphone, while his fur hat remains atop Gottwald’s head.
The Czech novelist Milan Kundera describes this scenario in the opening of “The Book of Laughter and Forgetting,” before a protagonist observes that the “struggle of man against power is the struggle of memory against forgetting.” For Kundera, Clementis’ fur hat was both a symbol and photographic relic of how Czechoslovakia’s authoritarian regime distorted history.
In the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic, history in the form of Vladimír Clementis was inconvenient and he was eliminated from the 1948 photograph, less his fur hat. Of course, Clementis’ disappearance is just one example of a broader antagonistic response to history by ideologues and authoritarians. History makes them uncomfortable, sad, angry and embarrassed because it argues against entrenched narratives, precious origin myths and stories about perceived victimhood.
Easier, then, for those in power to reprise their own versions of the opening scene from “The Book of Laughter and Forgetting,” symbolic fur hat of forgetting and all. But it is dangerous to ignore history, because doing so disregards a fundamental cause-effect truth described by the German writer Bernhard Schlink: “The tectonic layers of our lives (in other words, history) rest so tightly one on top of the other that we always come up against earlier events in later ones, not as a matter that has been fully formed and pushed aside, but absolutely present and alive.” 
“Absolutely present and alive”: The past lives on, despite our attempts to deny it— as in Mississippi, where the forces of forgetting that animated authoritarians in the Czechoslovak Socialist Republic are alive and well. Here, many of those who hold political and economic power insist on wearing magical hats of historical amnesia, substituting an antebellum “plantation owner’s” straw hat for Clementis’ Commie fur hat. 
Kundera described the state-sponsored historical amnesia of Stalinist Europe as “organized forgetting.” But the phenomenon also occurs in Mississippi, where it works to misinterpret or ignore the state’s racial history.
In Mississippi, organized forgetting results from an interaction between attitudes embedded in the state’s cultural DNA and government policy. Here, organized forgetting means repeatedly vandalizing the plaque memorializing Emmett Till’s death, and flying “Stars and Bars” battle flags.
It means celebrating Robert E. Lee’s Birthday on the same day as Martin Luther King’s Birthday, along with state holidays honoring Jefferson Davis and Confederate Memorial Day. It means electing a governor who annually proclaims Confederate Heritage Month (ignoring the slavery part), while arguing that “There is not systemic racism in America.” It means electing a United States senator who joked about a “public hanging” in a state where roughly 580 lynchings, primarily of Black people, occurred between 1882 and 1968. It means a legislature that in 2025 passed a ban on teaching “divisive concepts” about race and prohibited DEI programs in public education. It means continuing policies that perpetuate the state’s poverty rate, which is the highest in the United States. It means a new, highly regressive tax structure that will heighten income inequality and disproportionately affect Black people. 
Organized forgetting also means that the state GOP has fast-tracked redistricting following the Callais vs. Louisiana Supreme Court decision to diminish Black voting power, as in the Jim Crow era.
“Back to the Future,” circa 1890, when the president of Mississippi’s constitutional convention, S. S. Calhoon, stated that the constitution was being rewritten to “… exclude the Negro. Nothing short of this will do.” Now, Tate Reeves and others in the GOP explain that one goal of redistricting is to eliminate Congressman Bennie Thompson’s district, with Thompson being the only Black member of Congress from the state. Reeves has argued that the Callais decision “is a win for our Constitution and a tremendous win for our republic.” 
“To secure a lie,” writes Lewis Hyde, “surround it with a moat of forgetfulness.”
Thankfully in Mississippi there are institutions working against forgetting, including the Mississippi Civil Rights Museum, the Emmett Till Interpretive Center and the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument. But in our state there are not enough equivalents to the German “Stolpersteine,” or “stumbling stones”: about 70,000 small memorials to victims of the Holocaust, scattered across Europe. Here, there is insufficient collective resistance to forgetting, although the “tectonic events” of Mississippi’s racial history are “absolutely present and alive.” 
Of course, organized forgetting is present throughout our country, where the “Book of Forgetting” (minus the laughter) manifests itself in many of the Trump Administration’s actions: establishing the 1776 Commission as a response to the New York Times’ 1619 Project on the effects of slavery; eliminating funding for schools that teach “divisive, race-centered ideology” or “white privilege,” and attacking DEI programs. Among the institutions and organizations targeted are the National Museum of African American History and Culture, the American Women’s History Museum, the National Park Service and the Smithsonian American Art Museum. The Trump administration attacks historical memory that it deems “divisive” or “revisionist” because that history makes it uncomfortable and conflicts with stories about when and for whom America was “great.” 
The problem with forgetting history is that although doing so might support entrenched political and economic power, it perverts our understanding of both the past and present, and distorts our imagined futures. In Mississippi, as elsewhere, forgetting often represents an active refusal to know, which as the philosopher Karl Popper wrote, issues “from cowardice, pride or laziness of mind.” For Popper, “ignorance has an ethical dimension, and knowing is a moral obligation for human beings.” 
Actively embracing a past that never existed inhibits adaptation to the world created by our history. As the historian Timothy Snyder observes, “to abandon the search for understanding (is to) abandon history.” And to abandon history is to abandon hope of healing and positive change. Instead, we remain “victims of our own incomprehension,” bound to repeat past mistakes and make new and equally harmful ones. 
A flawed aspect of human nature is a deep-seated resistance to understanding the past, in all its uncomfortable complexity. So, although one quote widely but wrongly attributed to William Faulkner is apparently apocryphal, it remains devastatingly accurate, whether we’re talking about the United States, Communist Czechoslovakia or anywhere else on this earth: “To understand the world, you must first understand a place like Mississippi.”
And here, the hats of forgetting are everywhere: thousands of them, worn by politicians and the economic elite, worn by people who should know better, worn by those willing to follow them into darkness. 

Christopher Norment holds a PhD in Systematics and Ecology from the University of Kansas and is an emeritus professor of environmental science and ecology at the State University of New York–Brockport. During his career he published over 50 peer-reviewed scientific papers and three science-related books of creative nonfiction, and received awards from the State University of New York for teaching and scholarship. He now lives in Jackson.

name: California
title: California sues to stop National Archives closure that tribes say came without warning
text:
In summary
California says closure would endanger tribal records, including boarding school files. Tribes say they weren’t consulted. 


 The state of California filed a federal lawsuit against the National Archives and Records Administration on Oct. 14 seeking to keep open a facility whose closure was abruptly announced with no tribal, state or local consultation. 
In late September, the records administration announced the closing of two locations, the San Francisco and Chicago National Archives. Tribal governments depend on the National Archives for records relating to the Bureau of Indian Affairs including enrollment records, land records and deeds, federal boarding school records and more.
“Closing the National Archives at San Francisco … would irreparably harm California and its interests,” reads the lawsuit, filed in the U. S. District Court for the Northern District of California. “Indeed, transferring the records … would not only take them away from the communities that rely on them most, but also would risk damage and loss of the items altogether, given their age and fragility. At the very least, transferring the records means they would be inaccessible for an unknown period of time, which could last years, during transit and processing.”
California is home to 109 federally recognized tribes. 
California’s lawsuit asks the court to force the archives to halt the San Francisco facility closure. It was filed the same day as major national Native advocacy organizations slammed the planned closures in a letter sent to the former acting and current archivist of the United States.
Both the San Francisco Archives, which is located in neighboring San Bruno, and Chicago National Archives locations are slated to close at an unspecified date, though records could begin to move to other locations as early as next week, said California Attorney General Rob Bonta during a press conference Wednesday. 
The National Archives and Records Administration did not immediately respond to requests for comment. 
Tribal leaders and historic preservation officers said they’ve been continuously left in the dark regarding the closures and that they were not consulted on the plans. Since the announced closures, however, the archive administration held two virtual “consultations,” one on Oct. 13 and one on Oct. 15.
The virtual tribal consultations were structured more like a “listening session,” said Sokaogon Chippewa Community Tribal Historic Preservation Officer Michael LaRonge, who added that a consultation is an important first step, and shouldn’t be substituted with a listening session. 
LaRonge and others in attendance said they felt that the closure decisions were already finalized.
“I’m getting a lot of non-answers,” Fallon Carey, digital archives director for the National Native American Boarding School Healing Coalition to ICT. “It feels a lot like lip service.” 
Carey, a citizen of the Cherokee Nation, attended the virtual meeting on Oct. 15. 
“I think there’s a transparency issue here and there’s a lack of trust, from what I gather,” Carey said. “Tribal leaders and community members are really concerned.”
For communities looking to heal from the trauma of the federal Indian boarding school era, losing access to these records is a major concern, Carey said. Many survivors are elders who don’t have the time to wait for the records to become available again or the resources to travel and see them in person before they’re inaccessible, she said. 
“I have seen it with my own eyes, I’ve experienced it in my own life. Having access to these records can be deeply healing, having access to your own histories,” Carey said. 
Both LaRonge and Carey said National Archives leaders agreed to move the Bureau of Indian Affairs records last, but LaRonge said that doesn’t change the fact that it is moving. 
“[That’s] great if you work for a tribe who has funds to send people down there, but we don’t,” LaRonge said. “They just kept dangling that carrot, like ‘Oh, well, if you can just come to the reading room, the research room is open, you can just make an appointment.’ But no, I can’t… It doesn’t feel like a good victory.”
Additionally, leaders were told bureau records are not a priority for digitization as they contain private information, LaRonge said. 
“You have a responsibility to digitize these records – it’s part of your fiduciary responsibility to tribes under treaty law, a right to make those things available to us if we need them, and you’re telling us that it’s not a priority for you,” LaRonge said. “How many times do the tribes have to be told this isn’t a priority for us.”
LaRonge said the Sokaogon Band submitted a letter to Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker’s office to express its concern over the closure. Unlike California, there are no federally recognized tribes within Illinois. The state of Illinois has not filed any lawsuit against the National Archives. 
“For Illinois, it feels like the tribes have been kind of left behind,” LaRonge said. 
Both affected archives locations contain records that could be crucial to federally terminated tribes seeking restoration or unrecognized tribes seeking recognition. In one case, the Chicago National Archives contains documents from the former Green Bay Agency which may be crucial in the ongoing fight to restore the Brothertown Nation of Wisconsin’s federal recognition status, Chairwoman Phylis Tousey told ICT. The tribe was federally terminated by an act of Congress in 1839. 
Amelia Schafer is ICT’s North Central Correspondent based in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. She is of Wampanoag and Montauk-Brothertown Indian Nation descent.

name: National
title: Democrats could flip legislative chambers, break GOP supermajorities, analysis finds
text:
Members of the New Hampshire state House meet during session this May. Both of New Hampshire’s legislative chambers are considered among the most competitive this midterm election cycle, according to a recent analysis by Sabato’s Crystal Ball. (Photo by Molly Rains/New Hampshire Bulletin)Party control is up for grabs in 15 state legislative chambers across the country as Republicans are increasingly on the defensive this midterm election cycle, a new analysis found. 


2026’s most competitive legislative chambers
These are the state chambers considered most competitive by Sabato’s Crystal Ball Senior Columnist Louis Jacobson:
Alaska House
Alaska Senate
Arizona House
Arizona Senate
Georgia House
Maine House
Michigan House
Michigan Senate
Minnesota House
Minnesota Senate
New Hampshire House
New Hampshire Senate
Pennsylvania Senate
Wisconsin Assembly 
Wisconsin Senate
Source: Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics


The nonpartisan newsletter Sabato’s Crystal Ball at the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics released its final analysis of state legislative races ahead of November. Senior Columnist Louis Jacobson changed projections for 10 chambers — all shifting in favor of Democrats.
“In many states, Democrats are looking forward to a favorable year driven by a reaction to President Donald Trump and his policies,” he wrote.
Of the 15 competitive chambers this cycle, nine are currently controlled by Republicans and three are controlled by Democrats. Both of Alaska’s legislative chambers are controlled by bipartisan coalitions and the Minnesota state House is split evenly. 
Jacobson said Democrats may make inroads even in states not considered competitive. In 15 chambers expected to remain in Republican control, for example, he said Democrats could chip away at majorities or break GOP supermajorities — when a party has enough votes to override a veto. Those chambers include the Georgia state Senate, the Indiana state House, the Kansas state House and both chambers in Florida, Iowa, Missouri, North Carolina, Ohio and Texas.
In addition to winning control of the U.S. Congress, Democrats are looking to flip hundreds of state legislative seats this November following years of Republican dominance in statehouses. In addition to controlling a majority of governor’s offices, the GOP has held a majority of state legislative seats and chambers since 2010.
This year’s state legislative races are the third most competitive since 2010, according to Ballotpedia. The nonpartisan political encyclopedia measures competitiveness as the extent of choice available to voters: “More open seats, more contested primaries, and more races where both major parties field candidates mean more meaningful decisions on the ballot.”
Voters across 46 states will vote on 6,137 state legislative races next month. Of those races, 4,052 seats — 66% — are contested by both major parties. Ballotpedia found that 1,156 incumbents faced contested primaries this cycle — higher than its 16-year average.
