name: Missouri Independent
title: New Missouri nonprofit pours $2.9 million into campaign to reinstate abortion ban
text:
Supporters of Missouri's Amendment 3, which would reinstate a near-total abortion ban and place a permanent ban on gender-affirming care for minors into the constitution, gather for an informational meeting on Sept. 10 in St. Louis County (Anna Spoerre/Missouri Independent).A new Missouri-based nonprofit has dropped $2.9 million into a campaign hoping to reinstate an abortion ban. 
Her Health Her Future Missouri was incorporated in September and is now the top donor to Her Health, Her Future PAC, the campaign aimed at passing Amendment 3. If approved by a majority of voters, it would overturn the state’s 2024 reproductive-rights amendment.
The donations doubled the total amount of money the campaign had on hand as of Thursday, according to disclosure reports filed with the Missouri Ethics Commission. The campaign has raised $5.3 million since launching last year.
As a nonprofit, Her Health Her Future is not legally required to disclose its donors. Among its leadership are veterans of Missouri Republican politics, including Edward Greim, a partner at the Kansas City law firm Graves Garrett Greim; Michael Hafner, a longtime GOP consultant; and James Lawson, who is on a leave of absence from the Missouri Attorney General’s Office to serve as campaign adviser for Her Health Her Future PAC. 
Lawson said the nonprofit was formed to protect Missouri donors who wanted to give to the anti-abortion campaign “without putting a target on their backs.” 
Leaders with both campaigns have recounted instances of threats and harassment over their stances on abortion.
Lawson said “99%” of funding across the nonprofit and the PAC is from Missourians, noting that opponents of Amendment 3 have accepted millions from out-of-state nonprofits that also don’t disclose their donors.
“The real concern is outside money attempting to influence Missouri’s constitution,” Lawson said. 
Transgender care takes center stage in Missouri campaign to reinstate abortion ban

As of Thursday, Stop the Ban, the campaign pushing to defeat Amendment 3, has raised more than $25.7 million. A spokesperson with the campaign did not respond to a request for comment by time of publishing.
The Fairness Project, a D.C.-based nonprofit that backs progressive ballot measures around the country, has given nearly $12 million to Stop the Ban, whose leadership has pushed back on critics of its donors, saying The Fairness Project plays a supporting role to campaign efforts led by Missourians on the ground, including the local Planned Parenthood affiliates, Abortion Action Missouri, the ACLU of Missouri, PROMO and Beacon Reproductive Health Network. The Fairness Project is the only out-of-state group that sits on Stop the Ban’s executive committee. 
Alyssa Bowen, deputy executive director of True North Research, a progressive government accountability group not affiliated with either campaign, said because Her Health Her Future Missouri isn’t required to disclose its donors, it’s not possible for voters to know whether out-of-state anti-abortion voices end up throwing their money at Missouri. 
“These anti-abortion networks might be trying to position themselves as underdogs because of how much money the pro-choice side is spending on the issue, but that’s not an accurate depiction,” Bowen said.
Bowen, who supports abortion rights, noted there are far fewer donors to the anti-abortion campaign.
While the majority of Stop the Ban’s funding comes from out-of-state donors, thousands of Missourians have given small donations — any amount under $5,000 — to the cause. Nearly all of the reported donors to Her Health Her Future, are Missourians, but there are far fewer total donors.
In 2024, Missouri’s abortion rights campaign raised more than $30 million, handily outspending a hodgepodge of anti-abortion campaign efforts. Ultimately, the abortion-rights measure won with 51.6% of the vote.
Amendment 3 would repeal the 2024 reproductive rights amendment and reinstate an abortion ban with exceptions for fetal anomalies, medical emergencies and rape and incest in the first trimester. It would also enact a constitutional ban on gender-affirming care for minors. Missouri law bars minors from surgery, and from beginning hormones or puberty blockers; the latter law is set to expire in August 2027 at which point lawmakers could decide whether to extend it.
Lawson said Her Health Her Future Missouri was established to exist beyond the election, with the goal of educating Missourians on abortion and advocating for women and children.
Missouri Right to Life PAC is also campaigning for Amendment 3. So far the group has raised at least $800,000. 
On Tuesday, former Missouri Attorney General Andrew Bailey, who recently stepped down from his post as co-deputy director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation, filed for the creation of a PAC called Vote Yes on Amendment 3. No donations have yet been reported, but the PAC had already started purchasing broadcast ads as of Friday.
Less than three weeks out from the election, Stop the Ban had purchased more than half the broadcast air time among all ballot measure campaigns.
As of Thursday, Stop the Ban has spent about $5.9 million on TV and radio ads running in markets across Missouri’s top markets, including Kansas City, St. Louis, Springfield and Columbia. Her Health, Her Future has spent about $1.2 million.

title: Slideshow mistake prompts T to disclose new delay to Red Line train procurement
text:
THE MBTA’S campaign to replace the entire Red and Orange Line fleets with brand-new subway cars might be old enough to enroll in high school by the time it’s completed.
T officials on Thursday disclosed, again, that it will take longer than expected to receive all of the new Red Line cars outlined in a contract the Patrick administration first awarded to Chinese manufacturer CRRC back in 2014. The agency is in fact still not sure when it will hit the completion milestone, but they are confident at this point it will be later than the end-of-2027 target set in the prior round of delays.
The latest disruption comes amid massive trade upheaval with China and scrutiny by the Trump administration. Last year, federal customs officials detained train cars shipped to the Port of Philadelphia while verifying the Chinese company’s compliance with a US law prohibiting the import of goods produced using forced labor.
That action in turn prompted CRRC to furlough more than 160 workers at the Springfield factory where the trains are assembled. After about six months, workers began returning in July.
Officials said Thursday that the facility now has a full workforce and about 40 cars on location. CRRC is still developing an updated timeline to accommodate the newest delays, and it plans to open a second assembly line early next year.
“It’s unfortunate that actions by the federal government have further delayed the delivery of these new cars,” said MBTA spokesperson Joe Pesaturo. “But the MBTA remains fully committed to getting them into service as quickly as possible. We’re working closely with CRRC to get production back on track, accelerate deliveries, and ensure every new car meets our high standards for safety and reliability.”
But the federal review is far from the only speedbump the project has encountered. Both the budget and the timeline have swelled multiple times because of manufacturing problems, the COVID-19 pandemic, and supply chain disruption.
Under Gov. Deval Patrick, the MBTA in 2014 first awarded a $566 million contract to CRRC, which significantly underbid other competitors and the T’s own estimates. At the time, officials projected that all new trains would be in service by 2023.
A series of delays followed, as did reports of problems at the Springfield facility building the train cars.
At the start of her term, Gov. Maura Healey tapped a team of specialists to examine the state’s contract with CRRC. They concluded that, while the procurement was rife with issues, it was better for the T to stick with CRRC than to try to pivot to a new manufacturer so far into the process.
In 2024, the MBTA’s board voted to waive tens of millions of dollars in penalties and to pay CRRC $148 million to cover cost increases that had emerged since the contract was first rewarded. The contract “reset,” as it was called it at the time, set a new deadline that all vehicles would be delivered by the end of 2027 and  increased the total value of the contract above $1 billion.
Now, that date appears no longer viable, T officials said Thursday.
All 152 of the new Orange Line cars outlined in the contract have already been delivered. As of July 15, the agency has “conditionally accepted” 68 of the 252 Red Line cars called for in the contract. Officials say, regardless of the delay, the vehicles are functioning well and overperforming the contract target for how long they should travel on average before experiencing any issues.
Chris Friend, interim executive director of the advocacy and watchdog group TransitMatters, said failures with train vehicles “are by far the number one cause of delay on the Red Line due to the age of the current set of cars.”
“We would like more clarity from the T on the new expected delivery timeline to provide more frequent and more reliable service to riders,” he said.
Brian Kane, executive director of the MBTA Advisory Board group that represents cities and towns who help fund the T, views the setback as the latest sign that the T inked a “bad deal.”
“The T doesn’t have a great track record of introducing new vehicle technologies and new vehicle manufacturers to the United States market,” he said. “This whole procurement has been done incorrectly from day one, and now we’re living with those consequences. It’s going to cost us an awful lot more money.”
News of the latest delay took an unusual route to the spotlight. At an MBTA board subcommittee meeting Thursday morning, Susan Woods, the agency’s deputy chief financial officer for capital finance, briefed a handful of T overseers about the agency’s recent major investments. One page of her presentation highlighted the Red and Orange Line procurement, and it included the line, “Project scheduled for completion of deliveries in FY32.”
None of the T board members in attendance asked questions about the CRRC section of the presentation. Later in the day, after several outlets including CommonWealth Beacon inquired about the apparent change, T officials said there had been a bit of a misunderstanding: FY32 is the projected end for the entire contract itself, including a warranty period and other closeout costs, not the date by which the agency expects to get the final cars.
But at the same time, MBTA officials acknowledged they will no longer meet the 2027 deadline. A new projection, they said, should be available this winter.
At some point Thursday, the T uploaded a revised version of the slideshow. The FY32 date now includes an asterisk and a message noting the prior error.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Who pays when a remote Alaska village can no longer stay?
text:
Damage in Kwigillingok from ex-Typhoon Halong is seen on Oct. 16, 2025. (Photo provided by the Alaska National Guard)In Kipnuk and Kwigillingok, schools in the flood zone remained closed. Homes swept away are still scattered across the tundra. Where crushing waves snapped essential boardwalks, the days now carry the drone of power tools worked by young Yup’iks determined to rebuild them. 
From a bird’s eye view, the land seems to signal it has finally relaxed. You’d have to look hard to see where wind and water once forced their way across the coastal channels—the wild grasses among the riverbends have since smoothed over. 
A year after the remnants of Typhoon Halong unleashed a historic fury across Alaska’s Lower Kuskokwim Delta, few of the estimated 1,500 evacuees have returned. The storm, which struck Oct. 11 and 12, 2025, claimed at least three lives, destroyed more than 150 homes and affected 45 other communities across Western Alaska. It all but upended the Native Village of Kipnuk and neighboring Kwigillingok, two Yup’ik villages separated by a stretch of delta fringe hugging the Kuskokwim Bay. The Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA, has provided rental assistance to nearly 200 households, but that relief expires in April. State officials now plan to request an extension that could stretch as far as October 2027.
Across Alaska, two tight-knit communities have scattered like marbles to cities where costs are high and traditional subsistence is next to impossible. Voting has been disrupted, and children struggle to adjust to unfamiliar schools.      
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 

In February and March, tribal members in Kwigillingok and Kipnuk voted to move their wetland villages entirely. For Kipnuk, 92 percent of participating voters supported the migration. For Kwigillingok, Dustin Evon, the village climate resilience coordinator, said the decision boiled down to a single fear: “Another storm.” 
When he was growing up in the village in the 1990s, Evon recalls hardly any swamps. The land was firm and there were hills. You could also count on the bay to turn to slush at the start of fall freeze-up—what kept stormy seas from spilling across the sedge meadows.
But over the past two decades, Arctic waters have become a vast, iceless expanse. Rolling waves waterlog riverbanks and accelerate permafrost melt. Today, Evon’s boyhood village is a marshy mess. The tundra hills have all collapsed, leveling with land that residents describe as stepping onto a waterbed.  
“It’s gonna take a while,” Evon said, his voice flat with the weight of the challenges ahead. 
For decades, Alaska’s frontline climate communities have grappled with two questions: Where to move? And who pays? 
In August, the Native Village of Kwigillingok took a bold approach, telling the U.S. Supreme Court that Big Oil should be the one to foot the bill.  
Flooded areas of the Yukon-Kuskokwim Delta are seen on Oct. 13, 2025. The view from the air was seen by Alaska Air National Guard rescue personnel who were conducting search and rescue operations in the region, which was hit by the remnants of Typhoon Halong. (Photo provided by Alaska Air National Guard)
***
Over the summer, a sprawling array of amicus briefs filled the docket in the landmark climate case, Suncor v. Boulder, a lawsuit testing whether the fossil fuel industry can face climate-damage claims under state law. The Colorado city of Boulder and surrounding Boulder County sued Canadian energy company Suncor and U.S. oil giant ExxonMobil, alleging the companies knowingly contributed to climate change while misleading the public about its dangers. Nearly 70 filings came from a diverse pool of state attorneys general, members of Congress, the petroleum industry, environmentalists and more.  
In an Aug. 3 brief supporting Boulder, Colorado, the Native Village of Kwigillingok joined twelve other federally-recognized tribes, including three Y-K Delta neighbors, Akiak, Akiachak and Kwethluk. Its message to the justices was both urgent and distinct: “It is accordingly no exaggeration to say that the very survival of many Alaska tribes and their cultures is at stake,” read the brief. 
Alaska’s acting attorney general, Cori Mills, however, joined a coalition of states backing the oil companies, arguing that state-law-related climate damages claims threaten states’ authority over energy policy. The position reflects a defining paradox for Alaska: a state heavily dependent on oil and gas revenues, yet warming three to four times faster than the global average, with nearly 65 percent of the state’s Indigenous population facing the prospect of displacement. 

Chronic riverbank erosion in Akiachak, Alaska in July 2025. (Photo by Jenni Monet)

The Supreme Court opened its new term Oct. 5, hearing Suncor, a complex dispute over whether Boulder’s climate-damages lawsuit can proceed under Colorado state law or are preempted by federal law leaving no grounds to sue. The outcome could affect more than 60 similar lawsuits nationwide, including one brought by the Makah and Shoalwater Bay tribes in Washington state court. Both lead the amicus brief joined by Kwigillingok. 
The lawsuits seek billions of dollars in damages from fossil fuel companies, alleging consumer product deception. The industry counters that these cases amount to an attempt to regulate emissions through litigation rather than Congress, which has never enacted a framework to hold energy giants liable for climate change.  
Should the conservative Court side with the oil industry, it could effectively shield fossil fuel companies from a growing wave of state-law climate-damages lawsuits, closing off a potentially vital path to compensation for communities like Kwigillingok. 
Such a ruling, warned legal advocates who joined the tribes, would expose a deep moral bankruptcy in the climate crisis: forcing ancient nations to shoulder the cost of securing an Indigenous future against a catastrophe they neither created nor can afford. 
Gerald Torres, a Yale professor who co-signed the brief with Kwigillingok, framed the issue as a test of the nation’s commitment to tribal sovereignty. “Without a means of securing the resources through litigation or legislation to address these issues, it challenges our commitment to tribal sovereignty and self-governance,” he said. 
A decision is not expected until next year.
***
Alaska embodies the contradictions at the heart of Suncor. As the nation’s fifth largest oil producer and home to 229 federally-recognized tribes, it is also among the fastest-warming places on Earth. It is also the birthplace of an early lawsuit seeking damages for climate change, which is considered a landmark case. 

 
Nearly two decades ago, in 2008, the Native Village of Kivalina sued 24 oil and energy companies, alleging that corporate deception over greenhouse gas emissions contributed to warming and the chronic erosion of their eight-mile-long island. Unlike Boulder, Kivalina brought its case under federal law. In 2012, the Ninth Circuit dismissed the suit, ruling that the Clean Air Act displaced federal common-law claims over greenhouse gas emissions, but it provided no means for the village to sue. The defeat helps explain why climate-damages litigation has increasingly turned to state law—and why Suncor matters.
Today, Kivalina is inching toward relocation along an eight-mile gravel road completed in 2021. At its end stands a new school tucked into the foothills of the Brooks Range where classes began the following year. Without this infrastructure, the village might still be marooned in its escape from the encroaching Chukchi Sea —trapped between a broken federal aid system and the improbable demands of funding its own protection.
In a text exchange, Millie Hawley, Kivalina’s tribal administrator, described what it takes to move a village: “Tremendous time and effort.”
On any given day, Hawley coordinates a patchwork of government officials, private consultants, archeologists, lawyers and the operators of the nearby Red Dog zinc mine. 
“Obtaining the funds to move a village is daunting,” she said. “But we expect no less from the agencies. After all, we are United States citizens as well as a tribal community under agreement with the United States Constitution.”
For two years, Hawley and the tribal council fought to secure state funding for the new school and access road. The project was already legally owed to them, but the 2015-2016 Republican-controlled state legislature resisted the cost, bristling at how the tribe had cleverly secured an emergency evacuation route through an unrelated civil rights settlement with the state. 
In one of Alaska’s more remarkable climate twists, Kivalina cleared a multi-million dollar infrastructure hurdle through, of all things, a school discrimination lawsuit—hardly a replicable model for relocation. A judge found that the state had systematically shortchanged rural, predominantly Indigenous schools in favor of mostly white, urban ones. The court-ordered remedy was a new school for Kivalina, ultimately forcing lawmakers to earmark $43 million for the project in a community already threatened by the encroaching sea.
A modular home to house teachers is trucked up an eight-mile-long school access road in Kivalina, Alaska in July 2022. (Photo by Jenni Monet)
Mike Dunleavy, then a Republican state lawmaker on the Senate Finance Committee, made several attempts to delay, reduce or roll back funding for Kivalina’s school, questioning what he called the “whole Kivalina concept.” Years later, as governor in the immediate aftermath of Halong, Dunleavy downplayed the role of climate change, describing the devastation across the delta as a wildly unexpected “act of God.” 
Two decades earlier, another Alaska lawmaker had taken a different approach. Mere months into her tenure in 2003, Senator Lisa Murkowski introduced a novel land swap to help the Native Village of Newtok escape the eroding banks of the Ninglick River. Through its Native corporation, the tribe traded 12,000 acres for higher ground nine miles upriver—land that, ancestrally, was already theirs. Though not entirely climate-driven, the bargain helped Newtok bypass a wall of bureaucratic gridlock to begin one of America’s first modern community-wide climate migrations.
But securing land was only the beginning. A generation later, Newtok’s move to Mertarvik was separating families and straining tribal governance. Jackie Schaeffer, who leads climate initiatives at the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium, described it as running “two communities and one government” and with no established framework to pull it off. At the 2024 Arctic Encounter conference in Anchorage, Newtok tribal member Carolyn George described the agony of remaining in the village to keep her job at the school while her husband and five daughters lived in Mertarvik. “Being alone, I get anxiety and I miss my girls,” she said.  “Especially at night.” 

Alaska National Guardsmen in Newtok on Sept. 22 clear storm debris left by Typhoon Merbok. The Guardsmen went to several communities that suffered flooding and damage from that storm. (Photo by 1st Lt. Balinda O’Neal/Alaska National Guard)

A year after ex-Typhoon Halong, Kipnuk and Kwigillingok are drawing lessons from Newtok and Kivalina as they contemplate their own futures. Neither community has determined what relocation will cost. Kipnuk is exploring land options, while Kwigillingok has deployed drones to identify suitable ground near its storm-ravaged village. According to Dustin Evon, one prospective site sits on federal land requiring an exchange similar to Newtok’s. “We can’t do anything until we have land,” he said, adding the tribe has already contacted Murkowski. 
But securing land is only the first hurdle. Neither village has a clear path to financing its migration. Federal disaster-recovery programs largely focus on repairing damaged communities and providing temporary housing, not building new villages. “The programs that we have for disaster recovery really can’t relocate a community with those types of funding,” said Jeremy Zidek, public information officer with the Alaska Division of Homeland Security and Emergency Management. 
As climate disasters multiply, communities compete for limited federal relief. For the majority of tribal governments across Indian Country, which lack local tax bases available to cities and states, the costs of resilience present an especially oppressive burden.
In 2006, the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers estimated moving Kivalina, Newtok and Shishmaref, another threatened village, would cost between $80 million and $200 million—roughly $160 million to $330 million in today’s dollars. But the cheapest scenarios assumed “co-location”—a concept of folding whole villages into existing towns rather than rebuilding them as distinct communities. In its 2024 Unmet Needs report, the Alaska Native Tribal Health Consortium rejected this approach as “nonviable,” citing the federal government’s mid-century Urban Relocation Program which uprooted Natives to American cities resulting in loss of land-based language and lifeways.  

 
The funding system offers little reassurance. The same report found that of $93 million in federal spending for Fiscal Year 2019, just $17 million reached Alaska’s 144 environmentally threatened communities. A separate Government Accountability Office analysis reinforced the disparity, finding that an annual average of $18.4 million reached these communities between 2016 and 2020. The money is scattered across agencies and programs, often requiring technical expertise and grant-writing capacity that small tribal governments can scarcely afford. 
Only two federal agencies—the Bureau of Indian Affairs, BIA, and the Department of Housing and Urban Development—have dedicated programs supporting community-wide migration.
The tribal brief in Suncor puts the shortfall in stark relief: From 2012 through 2024, the BIA’s Tribal Community Resilience program, TCR, awarded $368.5 million nationwide—a sum that wouldn’t even cover Kivalina’s $400 million upper-end projections, alone. In Alaska, the brief estimates that the BIA program has met just two percent of $5.5 billion in identified needs. 
And it seems this funding pipeline has since stalled. After years of recurring grant solicitations, the Bureau has issued no new TCR grants beyond the Fiscal Year 2024 cycle, and federal award data show no new grants in 2025, the first year of Trump’s second administration. The Native Village of Akiachak confirms this lull as it still awaits $250,000 in erosion mitigation funding which was awarded under the Biden administration, as first reported by the Alaska Beacon. The BIA did not respond to a request for an explanation. 
Despite floodwaters rushing in, funding still flows at a trickle—and lost in this imbalance is precious time. 
***
In the second week of September, Rayna Paul, Kipnuk’s tribal administrator and environmental coordinator, returned to inspect the damage. Apart from a few hours in May, it was her first extensive tour of the village since Halong—the night she dodged flying debris in violent floodwaters to reach safety at the local school. On this trip, she spent several days on the ground and struggled to sleep each night. 
“It was a fast week with the inspectors, but it was still hard to see,” Paul said, describing the unearthed graves, missing boardwalks and severed power lines. Her home was among twenty or so that remain stranded along the distant riverbends like castaway ships.
FEMA and state officials accompanied Paul, assessing Kipnuk’s public infrastructure to determine its eligibility for recovery funding. Destroyed buildings could qualify for replacement; repairable structures, only rehabilitation. An initial assessment found that 95 percent of the village’s public infrastructure was a total loss. 
Across Western Alaska, the storm’s damage was initially estimated at $125 million. But Zidek said FEMA expects long-term recovery costs to exceed $250 million. The losses that cut deepest, however, will likely never appear on a federal balance sheet. 
“There’s that piece missing where we’re not even teaching our youth,” Paul said, describing the quieter erosion of traditional knowledge. “Like filling our freezers and teaching them how to cut a seal.” Paul picked up on this grief at the twice-monthly gatherings of storm survivors in Anchorage, where displaced villagers come together to laugh, commiserate and stay connected. But the reunions have turned bittersweet for the ways they reveal the hidden toll of being separated from homelands and one another. 
Rayna Paul, tribal administrator and environmental director for Kipnuk, testified before the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs, in Anchorage on May 5, 2026, urging federal lawmakers to support long-term relocation efforts for climate-threatened Alaska Native villages. (Photo by Jenni Monet/Alaska Beacon)
Paul said she dreams of an interim village where aunties and grandpas are only a few doors apart, where snowmachines and Honda ATVs—the all-terrain version of the family Buick—roam freely, and children can once again speak Yup’ik in the classroom. Perhaps in the Mat-Su-Valley, north of Anchorage. Perhaps with modest paths lined with tiny homes paid for, in part, by the tiny payouts from FEMA. A legal advocate for Kipnuk and Kwigillingok, Sheryl Musgrove, suggested that the $44,800 available through federal housing assistance might almost cover the cost of a single tiny home. 
But even the possibility of shelter comes with profound sacrifice. To leave Indigenous lands is akin to abandoning a relative.  
“We are losing our close ties and relationship to the lands,” Paul testified at a May field hearing in Anchorage, convened by Sen. Murkowski as chair of the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs. “Our heritage, our culture, our very way of life is under threat.”
Her warning carried well beyond that gathering. Though Kipnuk did not join the tribal brief in Suncor, its authors quoted Paul’s testimony directly, invoking her words to illustrate what was at stake for Alaska Native communities. Days later, Murkowski took to the U.S. Senate floor to recount the hearing and warn that public compassion could fade as the disaster slipped from the headlines. 
She recalled the terror of families whose homes had been swept from their foundations, spinning through white-capped waters with people still inside. “We should all be listening,” Murkowski told her colleagues. 
Alaska’s senior senator went on to criticize the Stafford Act and its federal disaster-recovery mandate that, she argued, pushes displaced communities back toward danger. “We’ll help you, but you have to return to the site of the tragedy,” she said, paraphrasing the government’s response. “Rebuild where you are.” 
Pointing to Newtok’s decades-long migration, she renewed calls for a lead federal agency to coordinate such moves. She also acknowledged the federal government’s historical role in forcing Native peoples into settlements that have since become increasingly vulnerable. This historic weight came through in her memoir as a debt still unresolved. “By every measure, the federal government owes it to the people to help them move to a new, safer place,” she wrote.
Yet, Murkowski’s position reflects a larger political contradiction. A longtime advocate for Alaska’s oil industry, she has called for greater responsibility in helping communities escape climate danger—but without embracing the tribal effort in Suncor to hold fossil fuel producers financially accountable. Her appeal for reform comes as federal disaster policy continues to leave communities like Kipnuk and Kwigillingok navigating an uncertain future with no clear means of financing migration. Murkowski was unavailable for comment. 
For Paul, the urgency extends far beyond Kipnuk. Her community has endured three federally declared disasters in a short span. And she knows: more storms are coming.  
“We’re paving a way to navigate through all of this,” she said. “These storms are not going to be the only ones, and we need to come together and sit down at the table and make the right decision for all Alaskans.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Appeals court permits Kansas law barring prefilled mail-in ballot applications
text:
A ballot drop box appears Oct. 12, 2026, in downtown Lawrence, Kansas. (Photo by Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector)TOPEKA — A federal appeals court for the second time reversed a prohibition on a Kansas law that bars organizations from prepopulating applications for mail-in ballots before the applications are sent to voters.
A three-judge panel for the 10th Circuit Court of Appeals found that a lower court didn’t strike down the law based on its justifications, text or legislative history.
“It instead inferred an improper purpose from the national political debate on mail-in voting,” the Wednesday decision said.
The Kansas Legislature passed in 2021 the prohibition on prefilling mail-in ballot applications, which also bars out-of-state organizations and individuals from distributing applications. Two voting rights organizations — VoteAmerica and the Voter Participation Center — challenged the law, suing Secretary of State Scott Schwab, Attorney General Kris Kobach and Stephen Howe, district attorney of Johnson County, arguing the state law infringed upon their free speech rights.
Voter Participation Center and its sister organization, nonprofits with the goal of boosting voter registration, sent partially prefilled mail-in ballot applications to about 510,000 Kansans in 2020, according to the decision. County officials expressed frustration that the prefilled ballot information didn’t match the state’s voter registration database.
The appeals panel rejected the Voter Participation Center’s argument that the law was created with the intent to suppress advocacy for mail-in voting.
“While we may reasonably infer that the enjoined distributor ban was enacted to restrict mail-in voting, we cannot infer that the ban was enacted to suppress speech supporting mail-in voting,” the 33-page decision said. “The ban prohibited the mailing of mail ballot applications, not messages supporting mail-in voting.”
The Voter Participation Center said it was “disappointed” in the decision, calling the underlying law “dangerous.”
“The provisions upheld by the court will make voting more difficult for Kansans by threatening their ability to vote-by-mail,” said Tom Lopach, president and CEO of the center.
“In the 2020 election, we saw firsthand the urgency of vote-by-mail in the midst of the pandemic. That’s why we fought back — to protect Kansans and their right to vote. We will keep working to ensure every American can make their voice heard.”
Honest Elections Project, a nonpartisan group with a history of advocating for restrictive voting laws, filed an amicus brief in the case in support of Schwab. Its executive director, Jason Snead, said the appeals court “got it right.”
“Judges cannot simply assume that legislatures acted in bad faith in order to kill reasonable, common sense election integrity laws,” Snead said. “Kansas acted after error-filled, prefilled mail-ballot applications flooded voters and overwhelmed county election officials in 2020. Protecting voters from confusion and keeping elections orderly is commonsense, not suspect.”
The court’s decision came after voter registration ended Tuesday and early voting began Wednesday for the Nov. 3 midterm elections.

name: California
title: Prop. 1 would generate billions for new housing. Here’s how it would be spent
text:
Construction on Casa Sueños, an affordable housing complex in Oakland, on Aug 7, 2023. Photo by Semantha Norris, CalMatters




California needs to build a lot more housing. But to do that, it’s going to need a lot of money. 
Proposition 1 would enable the state to borrow $11.25 billion for housing, but where exactly would the money go if it passes?
As CalMatters’ Marisa Kendall explains, Prop. 1 would fund housing for veterans, homeless Californians, renters, homeowners, farmworkers, students and tribes.
Most of the money, $7.2 billion, would be earmarked for buying, building or renovating apartment buildings. Projects would have to reserve a certain number of units for low-income households. 
Some housing would be set aside for homeless housing that includes additional services, known as “supportive housing.” This, in combination with other funding sources, would help support up to 40,000 rental units, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office. 
The office also estimates that Prop. 1 would cost the state up to $600 million a year for about 25 years to pay off the bond, including interest.
Proponents say that while it’s no silver bullet for the state’s housing crisis, it would help get some existing projects past the finish line. 
Nearly 40,000 affordable units throughout California have been designed, permitted and partially funded — but are stalled because developers can’t get enough money to build them, according to a recent report. Projects for homeless and low-income residents also need large subsidies since their tenants don’t pay enough in rent to offset building costs.
Some Republican lawmakers opposed the bill that placed the proposal on the ballot. Sen. Tony Strickland of Huntington Beach said the measure borrows “money against the future,” and that it would be risky to push the state deeper into debt.

Strickland, during a Senate floor vote in June: “There’s really no reason … other than to put hardworking families and the California taxpayers more in debt moving forward in perpetuity.” 

Read more.

Other Stories You Should Know


CA’s 100th lawsuit against Trump 2.0


Attorney General Rob Bonta at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Jan. 5, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters/Pool




From CalMatters’ Nigel Duara: 
California Attorney General Rob Bonta on Thursday filed the state’s 100th lawsuit against the federal government since President Donald Trump took office for a second time in 2025. 
Bonta reached that milestone in 21 months. During the first Trump administration, California officials sued the federal government a total of 123 times in four years. 
The lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Central District of California, alleges that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement overstepped its Constitutional limits by taking people into custody at state courthouses, a practice forbidden by a federal judge that ICE nevertheless continues to employ. 
The California Justice Department found ICE detained 34 people at state courthouses in June 2026. In July 2026, the month after the judicial order to stop making arrests at courthouses, ICE detained 28 people at courthouses. 

California Justice Department, in a statement: “ICE’s directive on courthouse enforcement and the resulting enforcement activities have had a profound chilling effect that has hindered California’s ability to enforce the law and protect public safety.”

More Trump lawsuits: In an extraordinary intervention leading up to the election, the Trump administration is suing California and Los Angeles County to try to force elections officials not to count potentially 20,000 registered voters’ ballots as it continues to look for evidence of noncitizens voting. Read more from CalMatters’ Jeanne Kuang and Ana B. Ibarra.



Outside groups pour big bucks into legislative races


Lawmakers gather on the Assembly floor at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Aug. 31, 2026. Photo by Fred Greaves for CalMatters




Powerful outside groups are pouring millions of dollars into competitive California legislative races this year to try and sway voters and ultimately shape the next Legislature, writes Calmatters’ Kate Wolffe.
Political action committees backed by cryptocurrency billionaires, tech companies and unions have spent almost $100 million on races so far this election cycle. These groups are not directly affiliated with the campaigns, and unlike direct contributions to candidates, there is no limit on how much these committees can spend.
Two new tech-backed groups have dominated spending in legislative races: Grow California, funded by a cryptocurrency investor and a venture capitalist, spent $17.5 million this cycle. California Leads, funded by Meta and Google, spent close to $14 million this year.
A CalMatters analysis found that since the June primary, tech PACs are driving up spending to elect more moderate candidates in four races — three of which are in solidly blue districts and the other in a purple district.
Read more.



And lastly: CA’s aging fishermen


A fisherman and a deckhand look off into the distance near the coast of La Jolla in San Diego on May 26, 2026. Photo by Adriana Heldiz, CalMatters




San Diego was once the tuna capital of the world, but only about 130 commercial fishermen remain in the county. An aging workforce, low pay and limited ways into the industry are making it difficult to attract newcomers. CalMatters’ Deborah Brennan and video strategy director Robert Meeks have a video segment on California’s shrinking fishing industry as part of our partnership with PBS SoCal. Watch it here.
SoCalMatters airs at 5:58 p.m. Fridays on PBS SoCal.






California Voices
CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: California passed two laws this session related to the state’s long-running “tort wars” — which pits personal injury lawyers and their allies against business interests and their insurers — and tort warriors are gearing up for the next round.
When a company lets a computer system arbitrate rental decisions, it can deny families access to housing and reinforce racial barriers with no accountability, writes Dillon Forst, a logistics coordinator who is studying at California State University, San Marcos.
